modules.title: 1. Getting Started: Interface & Workspace
modules.content:
## A First‑Look at Photoshop

Imagine you’ve just taken a photo of a sunrise that you want to turn into a striking social‑media header. You launch Photoshop, stare at a sea of icons, and wonder where to begin. The truth is, before you start drawing or retouching, you need to understand the **workspace**—the digital desk where every tool lives. This chapter walks you through every pane and button you’ll meet the first time you open Photoshop, shows you how to arrange them for a workflow that feels natural, and teaches the essential navigation tricks that let you move around your image with confidence. By the end, you’ll be able to open a file, zoom in on a detail, pan across the canvas, and save your work as a Photoshop Document (**.psd**)—the foundation for everything that follows.

---

## The Menu Bar: Your Command Center

At the very top of the screen sits the **Menu Bar**. Think of it as the “File → Edit → Image” ladder you can climb to access every function Photoshop offers. Each menu groups related commands, and most actions you’ll perform later—such as creating a new document, adjusting image size, or applying a filter—are found here.

| Menu | Primary Purpose | Typical First‑Time Use |
|------|----------------|------------------------|
| **File** | Create, open, close, and save documents | *File → New* to start a blank canvas |
| **Edit** | Undo/redo, cut/copy/paste, transform selections | *Edit → Transform* to resize a layer |
| **Image** | Adjust overall image properties (size, rotation, mode) | *Image → Image Size* to change resolution |
| **Layer** | Manage layers, create masks, blending options | *Layer → New → Layer* to add a blank layer |
| **Select** | Make, modify, and save selections | *Select → All* to highlight the whole canvas |
| **Filter** | Apply creative or corrective effects | *Filter → Blur → Gaussian Blur* for softening |
| **View** | Control what you see (rulers, guides, zoom) | *View → Show → Grid* to display a grid overlay |
| **Window** | Show or hide panels (Tools, Layers, Color, etc.) | *Window → Layers* to bring the Layers panel back |
| **Help** | Access Photoshop help topics and tutorials | *Help → Photoshop Help* for on‑demand guidance |

> **Tip:** Hovering over any menu item highlights a short description at the bottom of the screen. Use this “status bar” as a quick reference while you explore.

---

## The Options Bar: Contextual Controls

Directly beneath the Menu Bar is the **Options Bar**. Unlike the static Menu Bar, the Options Bar changes its contents depending on the tool you have selected. It provides the most immediate controls for that tool, letting you fine‑tune settings without digging into dialogs.

### What You’ll See

- **Brush Size & Hardness** when the Brush tool is active.
- **Opacity & Flow** for any painting or erasing tool.
- **Blend Mode** dropdown for layers (e.g., *Multiply*, *Screen*).
- **Shape Options** (fill, stroke) when a shape tool is chosen.

### Why It Matters

Because the Options Bar reflects the **current context**, you can see at a glance what parameters are affecting your work. Adjusting the **Opacity** to 50 % makes a brush stroke semi‑transparent, which is essential for creating subtle shading or building up color gradually.

---

## The Tools Panel: The Toolbox

Located on the left side of the default workspace, the **Tools Panel** houses the icons you’ll click to select drawing, selection, and navigation tools. Each tool is represented by a small picture (an icon) and often has a keyboard shortcut for faster access.

| Tool | Icon Description | Shortcut | Typical Use |
|------|------------------|----------|-------------|
| **Move** | Four‑arrow cross | **V** | Reposition layers or selections |
| **Marquee** (Rectangular/Elliptical) | Dashed rectangle/ellipse | **M** | Select rectangular or oval areas |
| **Lasso** (Lasso, Polygonal, Magnetic) | Free‑hand line | **L** | Draw custom selections |
| **Crop** | Two intersecting right angles | **C** | Trim edges of an image |
| **Eyedropper** | Pipette tip | **I** | Sample a color from the canvas |
| **Brush** | Paintbrush tip | **B** | Paint or paint‑like effects |
| **Eraser** | Rectangular eraser | **E** | Remove paint or mask pixels |
| **Hand** | Open palm | **H** | Pan (move) the view when zoomed |
| **Zoom** | Magnifying glass | **Z** | Zoom in/out of the canvas |

> **Note:** The Tools Panel can be collapsed or expanded by clicking the double‑arrow at its top. If you ever lose it, press **Tab** to hide all panels, then **Shift + Tab** to bring them back.

### Customizing the Tools Panel

You can **reorder** tools by dragging their icons, and you can **hide** tools you never use. Right‑click the panel’s header and choose *Customize Toolbar* to add shortcuts or reset to the default layout.

---

## The Layers Panel: The Stack of Your Work

On the right side of the screen sits the **Layers Panel**. Photoshop works on the principle of **layers**, which are like transparent sheets stacked on top of each other. Each layer can hold its own image data, text, or adjustment, and you can edit a layer without affecting the others.

### Core Components

- **Layer Thumbnail** – a miniature preview of the layer’s content.
- **Eye Icon** – toggles visibility; click to hide/show a layer.
- **Lock Icon** – prevents accidental changes; useful for background layers.
- **Opacity Slider** – controls the transparency of the whole layer.
- **Blend Mode Dropdown** – determines how the layer mixes with layers beneath it (e.g., *Overlay* adds contrast).

### Basic Layer Operations

1. **Create a New Layer** – Click the **New Layer** button (paper‑plus icon) or press **Shift + Ctrl + N** (Windows) / **Shift + Cmd + N** (Mac).
2. **Rename a Layer** – Double‑click the layer’s name (e.g., “Layer 1”) and type a descriptive title.
3. **Reorder Layers** – Drag a layer up or down to change its stacking position.
4. **Group Layers** – Select multiple layers, then click the **Folder** icon to create a group, keeping related layers together.

Understanding layers early on will save you countless hours later, as most editing tasks rely on manipulating them rather than altering the original image.

---

## Customizing the Workspace

Photoshop ships with several preset workspaces—*Essentials*, *Photography*, *Graphic and Web*, etc.—but you can tailor the layout to match your personal workflow. A well‑organized workspace reduces mouse‑travel, keeps the tools you need in sight, and speeds up learning.

### Step‑by‑Step Customization

1. **Show/Hide Panels**  
   - Go to **Window** in the Menu Bar.  
   - Click any panel name (e.g., *Color*, *History*) to toggle its visibility.  
   - Panels you open will dock on the right side by default; you can drag them to the left or float them as separate windows.

2. **Arrange Panels**  
   - Drag a panel’s tab to a new location.  
   - Drop it when you see a blue highlight indicating where it will dock.  
   - Create tab groups by dropping one panel onto another’s tab.

3. **Resize Panels**  
   - Hover over a panel’s edge until the cursor changes to a double‑arrow.  
   - Click and drag to make the panel wider or taller.

4. **Save Your Layout**  
   - Once you’re happy with the arrangement, choose **Window → Workspace → New Workspace…**  
   - Give it a name (e.g., “My Beginner Setup”).  
   - Check the boxes for *Workspace*, *Keyboard Shortcuts*, and *Menu* if you also want to preserve any custom shortcuts.  
   - Click **Save**.  

   Later, you can switch back to this layout anytime via **Window → Workspace → My Beginner Setup**.

### Quick‑Access Tips

- **Resetting to Default** – If you ever get lost, choose **Window → Workspace → Essentials** and then click **Reset Essentials**.
- **Full‑Screen Mode** – Press **F** to toggle between normal, full‑screen with menu bar, and full‑screen without menu bar. This removes distractions while you focus on the canvas.

---

## Navigating the Canvas: Zoom, Pan, and Hand Tools

Even the simplest image can become a maze when you zoom in to edit fine details. Photoshop offers several navigation tools that let you move around without altering the image itself.

### Zoom Tool (**Z**)

- **Click** once to zoom **in** (default 200 %).  
- **Alt‑click** (Windows) / **Option‑click** (Mac) to zoom **out**.  
- **Click‑drag** to draw a rectangle around the area you want to fill the screen with.  

> **Pro tip:** Hold **Ctrl** (Windows) / **Cmd** (Mac) while scrolling the mouse wheel to zoom continuously.

### Hand Tool (**H**)

- Activate the Hand tool, then **click‑drag** anywhere on the canvas to pan (move) the view.  
- When you’re zoomed in, you’ll often switch rapidly between **Zoom** and **Hand**.  

> **Shortcut trick:** While the **Zoom** tool is active, press the **Spacebar** to temporarily switch to the Hand tool. Release the spacebar to return to Zoom.

### Pan Using Scrollbars

If you prefer not to use the Hand tool, you can also click the horizontal or vertical scrollbars at the bottom and right edges of the canvas. However, the Hand tool is usually faster for precise navigation.

### Fitting the Image to the Screen

- **Fit on Screen** – Press **Ctrl + 0** (Windows) / **Cmd + 0** (Mac).  
- **Actual Pixels** – Press **Ctrl + Alt + 0** (Windows) / **Cmd + Option + 0** (Mac) to view the image at 100 % size.

---

## Opening, Closing, and Saving PSD Files

A **PSD** (Photoshop Document) is Photoshop’s native file format. It preserves all layers, masks, adjustment layers, and vector information, allowing you to return to a project later and continue editing.

### Opening a File

1. Choose **File → Open…** or press **Ctrl + O** (Windows) / **Cmd + O** (Mac).  
2. In the dialog, navigate to the folder containing your image.  
3. Select a **.psd** file, or any other supported format (JPEG, PNG, TIFF).  
4. Click **Open**.  
   - If the file contains multiple layers, they appear in the Layers panel exactly as they were saved.  

### Closing a Document

- **File → Close** or press **Ctrl + W** (Windows) / **Cmd + W** (Mac).  
- If you have unsaved changes, Photoshop prompts you to **Save**, **Don’t Save**, or **Cancel**.  

### Saving Your Work

1. **Save** – Choose **File → Save** or press **Ctrl + S** (Windows) / **Cmd + S** (Mac). This overwrites the existing file.  
2. **Save As** – To create a new version or change the file type, select **File → Save As…**  
   - In the dialog, give the file a new name if desired.  
   - Choose **Photoshop (*.PSD; *.PDD)** from the format dropdown to retain layers.  
   - Click **Save**.  

   > **Important:** Saving as a JPEG or PNG flattens the image—layers are merged, and you lose the ability to edit them later. Always keep a master **.psd** version.

3. **Version Control** – For beginners, a simple habit helps: after each major edit, use **Save As** with an incremental suffix (e.g., *sunrise_v01.psd*, *sunrise_v02.psd*). This creates a safety net and lets you compare versions.

### Quick‑Save Shortcut

- Press **Ctrl + Shift + S** (Windows) / **Cmd + Shift + S** (Mac) to open the **Save As** dialog instantly.

---

## Putting It All Together: A Mini Workflow

1. **Launch Photoshop** – The default **Essentials** workspace appears.  
2. **Open your sunrise photo** – *File → Open* → select *sunrise.jpg*.  
3. **Zoom in** to the horizon line – press **Ctrl + +** (or use the Zoom tool).  
4. **Pan** to the left edge – hold **Spacebar** (temporary Hand tool) and drag.  
5. **Create a new layer** – **Shift + Ctrl + N**, name it *Adjustment*, and click **OK**.  
6. **Select the Brush tool** – press **B**, choose a soft brush from the Options Bar, set **Opacity** to 30 %.  
7. **Paint** a subtle orange highlight on the sun.  
8. **Save** – *File → Save As*, name it *sunrise_edit.psd*, keep the PSD format.  

You have now navigated the canvas, used a tool, worked with layers, and saved a fully editable Photoshop file. All of this was possible because you understood where each piece of the interface lives and how to customize it for your needs.

---

## Key Takeaways

- The **Menu Bar** houses all commands; the **Options Bar** shows tool‑specific settings; the **Tools Panel** provides quick access to drawing and selection tools; the **Layers Panel** manages the stack of editable elements.
- You can **customize** panel arrangement, hide or show panels, and **save** a personal workspace for future sessions.
- **Zoom**, **Hand**, and **Pan** tools let you navigate any canvas size; shortcuts like **Ctrl + 0** (fit) and **Spacebar** (temporary hand) speed up the process.
- Opening, closing, and **saving as PSD** preserves every layer and adjustment, ensuring you can return to a project without loss of editability.
- Practicing the workflow—open a file, zoom, pan, create a new layer, make a simple edit, and save—builds the muscle memory essential for every Photoshop project.

modules.title: 2. Understanding Layers & Selections
modules.content:
### A Real‑World Problem: Fixing a Photo Without Damaging the Original  

You’ve just taken a portrait of a friend, but the background is distracting. You want to blur it while keeping the subject sharp, and you also need to brighten the eyes. The safest way to do this is to work on separate **layers** and use **selections** to isolate the parts you’re editing. By the end of this chapter you’ll know exactly how to set up those layers, name and organize them, and pick out the subject with the selection tools—all without ever altering the original image file.

---

## Why Layers Are the Backbone of Non‑Destructive Editing  

When you open a file in Photoshop you’re actually looking at a **canvas** that can hold many transparent sheets stacked on top of each other – those sheets are *layers*. Each layer can hold its own pixels, text, or adjustment, and you can change one layer without affecting the others. This is what makes Photoshop a **non‑destructive** editor: the original image stays intact, and you can always go back, tweak, or delete any change you’ve made.

* **Safety:** Mistakes are reversible.  
* **Flexibility:** Reorder layers to change the visual hierarchy.  
* **Control:** Apply blending modes, opacity, or filters to a single layer only.  

Think of layers like a stack of transparent acetate sheets in a studio. You can draw on the top sheet, erase it, or move it aside, and the drawing underneath never changes.

---

## The Layer Panel: Your Command Center  

If you followed the first chapter, you’ve already seen the **Layers Panel** on the right side of the workspace. It lists every layer in the current **.psd** file, showing a thumbnail, the layer name, and icons for visibility, lock status, and blending mode.

### Core Icons at a Glance  

| Icon | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| 👁️ | **Visibility** – click to hide/show the layer. |
| 🔒 | **Lock** – prevents accidental edits (can lock position, transparency, or all). |
| 🎚️ | **Opacity** – dim the layer’s overall strength (0 % – 100 %). |
| ⬜ | **Blend Mode** – determines how the layer mixes with those below (e.g., *Multiply*, *Screen*). |

Hovering over an icon shows a tooltip that tells you its function. You’ll use these icons constantly when you create, rename, reorder, hide, lock, and delete layers.

---

## Creating, Renaming, and Reordering Layers  

### 1. Adding a New Layer  

1. Click the **Create a new layer** icon (the sheet‑of‑paper button) at the bottom of the Layers Panel.  
2. A blank layer appears above the currently selected layer and is automatically named *Layer 1*.  

> **Tip:** If you want the new layer to inherit the blending mode or opacity of the layer beneath it, hold **Alt** (Windows) / **Option** (macOS) while clicking the icon.  

### 2. Renaming for Clarity  

1. Double‑click the layer’s name in the panel.  
2. Type a descriptive name (e.g., *Background Blur*, *Eyes Brightness*) and press **Enter**.  

> **Why rename?** Clear names let you locate a layer quickly, especially in projects with dozens of them.

### 3. Changing the Stack Order  

* **Drag‑and‑drop:** Click a layer and drag it up or down the list.  
* **Keyboard shortcuts:**  
  * **Ctrl + ]** (Windows) / **Cmd + ]** (macOS) → move the selected layer up one spot.  
  * **Ctrl + [** / **Cmd + [** → move it down.  

The order determines which layers cover others. The topmost layer is drawn last, so it appears in front.

---

## Hiding, Locking, and Deleting Layers  

### Visibility  

Click the eye icon to toggle a layer’s visibility. This is useful for checking how an edit looks without the layer’s influence.

### Locking  

Photoshop offers three lock options:  

| Lock Type | What It Does |
|-----------|--------------|
| **Transparency** | Prevents erasing or painting on transparent pixels. |
| **Image Pixels** | Stops any pixel changes (paint, erase, filters). |
| **Position** | Stops moving the layer with the Move tool. |
| **All** | Combines the three above. |

To lock, click the lock icon and choose the appropriate option from the dropdown.

### Deleting  

Select the layer and press **Delete** on the keyboard, or click the **Delete layer** trash‑can icon at the bottom of the panel. Photoshop will ask for confirmation if the layer contains content.

> **Caution:** Deleting a layer is permanent unless you undo (**Ctrl + Z** / **Cmd + Z**) immediately. For safety, consider hiding the layer first to see the effect before removing it.

---

## Non‑Destructive Editing with Adjustment Layers (A Quick Glimpse)  

While adjustment layers belong to a later chapter, it’s worth noting that they are themselves layers that apply color or tonal changes **without altering the pixels beneath**. Because they sit in the layer stack, you can enable/disable, reorder, or delete them at any time—another demonstration of Photoshop’s non‑destructive power.

---

## Selections: Isolating Parts of Your Image  

A **selection** is a temporary mask that tells Photoshop which pixels to affect. Anything outside the selection is ignored until you change or deselect it.

### Why Selections Matter  

* **Targeted edits:** Apply filters, adjustments, or paint only where you need them.  
* **Precision:** Combine simple shapes to outline complex objects.  
* **Efficiency:** Work faster by selecting once and applying multiple edits.

---

## The Three Core Selection Tools  

You already know the **Move**, **Marquee**, and **Lasso** tools from the first chapter. Here’s how they behave when you use them for selections.

### 1. Marquee Tools  

* **Rectangular Marquee** – creates a rectangular or square selection.  
* **Elliptical Marquee** – creates an oval or circular selection.  

**How to use:**  
1. Choose the tool from the Tools Panel.  
2. Click and drag on the canvas.  
3. Release the mouse to fix the selection.  

Hold **Shift** while dragging to constrain the shape (square or circle). Hold **Alt** (Windows) / **Option** (macOS) to draw from the centre outward.

### 2. Lasso Tools  

* **Lasso** – freehand drawing of any shape.  
* **Polygonal Lasso** – click to create straight‑line segments; double‑click to close.  
* **Magnetic Lasso** – snaps to edges with high contrast, great for objects with clear outlines.  

**How to use the Magnetic Lasso:**  
1. Click a point on the edge you want to trace.  
2. Move the cursor along the edge; Photoshop automatically adds points when the contrast changes.  
3. Click again to add a manual point if needed, or press **Enter** to close the selection.  

### 3. The Move Tool (When Paired with Selections)  

When a selection is active, the **Move tool** lets you reposition only the selected pixels. This is handy for aligning objects without affecting the rest of the image.

---

## Building a Selection Step by Step  

Let’s walk through selecting the subject’s face in a portrait.

1. **Start with the Elliptical Marquee**  
   * Choose the Elliptical Marquee tool.  
   * Hold **Shift** + **Alt** and drag from the center of the face outward to get a perfect circle that roughly covers the head.  

2. **Refine with the Lasso**  
   * Switch to the **Polygonal Lasso**.  
   * Click at the jawline, then at the chin, and finally back at the starting point to add the lower contour.  

3. **Add the Hair**  
   * Activate the **Magnetic Lasso**.  
   * Click just above the forehead and trace along the hairline. The tool will cling to the edge of the hair.  

4. **Combine the Shapes**  
   * As you add new paths, Photoshop automatically **adds to** the existing selection (the default mode).  

5. **Fine‑Tune**  
   * Press **Q** to enter **Quick Mask mode** (a red overlay appears).  
   * Use a soft brush to paint over areas you want to include (white) or exclude (black).  
   * Press **Q** again to exit; your refined selection is ready.  

> **Tip:** If you accidentally include too much, hold **Alt** (Windows) / **Option** (macOS) while using a selection tool to **subtract** from the current selection.

---

## Selection Modifiers: Adding, Subtracting, Intersecting  

Photoshop lets you change how a new selection interacts with the existing one. The **Options Bar** (just below the menu bar) contains three icons for this purpose:

| Icon | Action |
|------|--------|
| ![Add to selection icon] | **Add to** – new area is added to the current selection. |
| ![Subtract from selection icon] | **Subtract from** – new area is removed from the current selection. |
| ![Intersect with selection icon] | **Intersect with** – only the overlapping region remains selected. |

You can also use keyboard shortcuts:  

* **Shift** → *Add to*  
* **Alt** (Windows) / **Option** (macOS) → *Subtract from*  
* **Ctrl** (Windows) / **Cmd** (macOS) → *Intersect with*  

### Practical Example: Selecting a Person Wearing a Hat  

1. **Select the hat** with the Elliptical Marquee (Add to).  
2. **Switch to Subtract** and use the Polygonal Lasso to cut out the interior of the hat where the head shows.  
3. **Switch to Intersect** and draw a rough rectangle around the whole figure; only the overlapping area (the hat plus head) stays selected.  

Now you have a clean selection that isolates the entire subject.

---

## Managing Selections: Saving, Loading, and Deselecting  

### Saving a Selection  

1. With the selection active, go to **Select > Save Selection…**.  
2. In the dialog, give it a name (e.g., *SubjectMask*) and click **OK**.  
3. The selection is stored as an **alpha channel** in the Channels Panel, where you can reload it later via **Select > Load Selection…**.  

### Deselecting  

Press **Ctrl + D** (Windows) / **Cmd + D** (macOS) to remove the active selection.  

### Inverting a Selection  

If you need everything *except* the current area, choose **Select > Inverse** or press **Shift + Ctrl + I** / **Shift + Cmd + I**.

---

## Putting It All Together: A Mini Workflow  

Imagine you need to brighten the eyes and blur the background of a portrait.

1. **Create a new layer** above the background and name it *Background Blur*.  
2. **Select the background**:  
   * Use the Elliptical Marquee to roughly cover the whole image.  
   * Switch to Subtract and use the Lasso to carve out the subject’s head and shoulders.  
3. **Apply a blur**:  
   * With the background selected, go to **Filter > Blur > Gaussian Blur** and set a radius that looks natural.  
4. **Hide the selection** (Ctrl + D).  
5. **Create another new layer** named *Eyes Brightness*.  
6. **Select the eyes**:  
   * Zoom in, use the Polygonal Lasso to outline each eye, then hold **Shift** to add the second eye to the selection.  
7. **Adjust brightness**:  
   * Choose **Image > Adjustments > Brightness/Contrast** (or later, an adjustment layer) and increase the brightness slightly.  
8. **Toggle visibility** of each layer to compare the before/after effect.  

Because each edit lives on its own layer, you can now go back, change the blur amount, or delete the *Eyes Brightness* layer without touching the original photo.

---

## Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them  

| Issue | Why It Happens | Fix |
|-------|----------------|-----|
| **Accidentally painting on the wrong layer** | The wrong layer is selected or visible. | Always check the active layer highlighted in the Layers Panel before drawing or painting. |
| **Selection “jumps” when moving the mouse** | The selection mode (Add/Subtract/Intersect) is unintentionally changed. | Keep an eye on the **Options Bar** icons; press **Esc** to reset to *Add to* if unsure. |
| **Locked layers preventing edits** | The lock icon is engaged, often from a previous step. | Click the lock icon to unlock, or choose the specific lock type you need to disable. |
| **Too many layers cluttering the panel** | Every minor edit was made on a new layer without naming or grouping. | Rename layers descriptively, and later group related layers (right‑click → **Group from Layers**). |
| **Selections becoming “fuzzy” after scaling** | Scaling a layer after a selection can introduce anti‑aliasing artifacts. | Perform scaling before making the selection, or use **Smart Objects** (covered later). |

---

## Quick Reference Cheat Sheet  

- **Create layer:** `Shift + Ctrl + N` (Windows) / `Shift + Cmd + N` (macOS)  
- **Rename layer:** Double‑click name → type → `Enter`  
- **Hide/show layer:** Click eye icon or press `Alt + click` on eye to hide all others  
- **Lock layer:** Click lock icon → choose lock type  
- **Delete layer:** Select → `Delete` or click trash can  
- **Select all:** `Ctrl + A` / `Cmd + A`  
- **Deselect:** `Ctrl + D` / `Cmd + D`  
- **Add to selection:** Hold **Shift** while drawing  
- **Subtract from selection:** Hold **Alt** / **Option** while drawing  
- **Intersect selection:** Hold **Ctrl** / **Cmd** while drawing  
- **Quick Mask:** `Q` (enter/exit)  

---

## Practice Exercise  

1. Open a portrait of your choice.  
2. Create three layers named *Background Blur*, *Skin Smooth*, and *Eyes*.  
3. Use the selection tools and modifiers to isolate the background, the skin, and the eyes respectively.  
4. Apply a Gaussian blur to *Background Blur*, a **Surface Blur** (later chapter) to *Skin Smooth*, and increase the brightness of *Eyes*.  
5. Toggle each layer’s visibility to see the before/after effect.  

When you’re comfortable, experiment with renaming, reordering, and locking the layers to observe how the image changes.

---

## Frequently Asked Questions  

**Q: Can I select a layer directly without using a selection tool?**  
A: Yes. Click the layer’s thumbnail in the Layers Panel to make it active. If you need a pixel‑perfect selection of that layer’s opaque areas, hold **Ctrl** / **Cmd** and click the thumbnail; Photoshop will load a selection based on the layer’s transparency.

**Q: What’s the difference between a selection and a mask?**  
A: A selection is temporary and disappears when you deselect. A mask is a permanent (but editable) channel that lives with the layer. Masks will be covered in Chapter 5.

**Q: Why does the Lasso tool sometimes behave unpredictably?**  
A: The tool follows the cursor’s speed and pressure (if using a tablet). For smoother curves, try the **Pen tool** (covered later) or adjust the **tolerance** in the Options Bar for the Magnetic Lasso.

---

## Summary  

- Layers let you edit parts of an image independently, enabling non‑destructive workflows.  
- The Layers Panel is where you create, rename, reorder, hide, lock, and delete layers.  
- Selections define *where* edits happen; the Marquee, Lasso, and Move tools are your primary selection instruments.  
- Selection modifiers (add, subtract, intersect) let you combine simple shapes into complex selections.  
- Saving selections as channels preserves them for later use.  

By mastering layers and selections now, you’ll have a solid foundation for every Photoshop project that follows.

---

## Key Takeaways  

- **Layers are independent transparent sheets**; edit them without altering the original image.  
- **Create, rename, and reorder** layers to keep your workspace organized and intuitive.  
- **Hide or lock** layers to safeguard work and focus on specific elements.  
- **Marquee, Lasso, and Move** tools are the core instruments for making and adjusting selections.  
- Use **Shift, Alt/Option, and Ctrl/Cmd** to **add, subtract, or intersect** selections while drawing.  
- **Save selections** as alpha channels for reuse; **deselect** with **Ctrl + D / Cmd + D**.  
- Practicing a simple workflow—isolating background, skin, and eyes—will cement these concepts and prepare you for more advanced techniques later.

modules.title: 3. Working with Colors & Brushes
modules.content:
## A Splash of Color: Why Choosing the Right Hue Matters  

Imagine you’ve just taken a photo of a sunrise and want to add a hand‑drawn “sun” that matches the warm tones of the sky. The difference between a flat orange circle and a vibrant, gradient‑rich sun is often just the way you pick and apply colors. In Photoshop, mastering **foreground** and **background** colors is the first step toward any creative brush work—whether you’re sketching, retouching, or adding simple accents.

---

## Selecting Colors  

Photoshop gives you three fast ways to tell the program which color you want to paint with. All three live in the **Tools Panel** and are reflected in the **Options Bar** at the top of the screen.

### 1. The Color Picker (Foreground/Background Swatches)  

1. **Locate the swatches** – In the lower part of the Tools Panel you’ll see two overlapping squares. The top (solid) square is the **foreground color** (the color you’ll paint with). The bottom (hollow) square is the **background color** (used by tools such as the Paint Bucket).  
2. **Open the Color Picker** – Click either swatch. A dialog called the **Color Picker** appears.  
3. **Choose a hue** –  
   * **Hue bar** (vertical on the right) selects the color family.  
   * **Saturation/value square** (large area) refines the exact shade.  
   * **Hexadecimal field** (bottom) lets you type a web color code (e.g., `#FF5733`).  
4. **Confirm** – Click **OK**. The swatch updates to show your new color.  

> **Tip:** Double‑click a swatch to open the Color Picker instantly, even if the tool you’re using isn’t a brush (e.g., the Eraser).

### 2. Swatches Panel – Quick Access to Favorites  

If you often reuse the same colors, the **Swatches** panel (Window → Swatches) is a visual palette of saved colors.

* **Add a swatch** – After picking a color with the Color Picker, click the **New Swatch** button at the bottom of the panel.  
* **Apply a swatch** – Simply click a swatch; the foreground color updates automatically.  
* **Organize** – Drag swatches to reorder them, or create groups for project‑specific palettes.  

> **Tip:** Photoshop ships with a set of “Web Safe” swatches. For print‑oriented work, you may want to create a custom set that matches your brand colors.

### 3. Eyedropper Tool – Grab Color Directly from the Image  

The **Eyedropper** (shortcut **I**) lets you sample any pixel on the canvas.

1. **Select the Eyedropper** from the Tools Panel.  
2. **Click** on the area whose color you want to capture. The foreground swatch instantly changes to that exact hue.  
3. **Sample multiple points** – Hold **Shift** and click additional spots; Photoshop will average the colors.  

> **Tip:** If you need a soft, blended sample (e.g., for a gradient sky), set the **Sample Size** in the Options Bar to **3 × 3** or **5 × 5** pixels.

---

## Getting Comfortable with the Brush Tool  

Now that you have a color, it’s time to bring it to life. The **Brush Tool** (shortcut **B**) is the workhorse for painting, retouching, and even creating masks.

### Accessing the Brush Settings Panel  

* **Open the panel** – Choose **Window → Brush Settings**.  
* **Why a separate panel?** – While the **Options Bar** lets you adjust size and hardness on the fly, the Brush Settings panel gives deeper control over shape, dynamics, texture, and more.

### Core Brush Controls  

| Setting | What It Does | Typical Use |
|---------|--------------|-------------|
| **Size** | Diameter of the brush tip (in pixels). | Large strokes for backgrounds, small for details. |
| **Hardness** | Edge sharpness (0 % = soft feathered edge, 100 % = crisp edge). | Soft edges for natural media effects; hard edges for graphic lines. |
| **Spacing** | Distance between consecutive brush marks when you drag. | Low spacing (1–5 %) for smooth lines; high spacing (10 %+) for dotted or stippled effects. |
| **Shape Dynamics** | Varies size, angle, or roundness based on pen pressure or direction. | Useful with graphics tablets for pressure‑sensitive brushwork. |
| **Texture** | Applies an image‑based texture to the brush tip. | Simulates charcoal, fabric, or custom patterns. |

> **Note:** Opacity and Flow are still controlled from the Options Bar. Opacity limits the overall transparency of each stroke, while Flow determines how quickly the paint builds up as you drag.

### Painting Simple Strokes – A Step‑by‑Step Walkthrough  

1. **Set your foreground color** – Use any of the three methods described earlier.  
2. **Select the Brush Tool** – Press **B** or click the brush icon.  
3. **Adjust size & hardness** –  
   * Quick change: Use the **[ ] brackets** on the keyboard (`[` reduces size, `]` increases).  
   * For finer control, click the **Size** or **Hardness** icons in the Options Bar and drag the sliders.  
4. **Create a stroke** – Click once to place a dot, or click‑drag to draw a line. Release the mouse button to finish.  
5. **Undo mistakes** – Press **Ctrl+Z** (Windows) or **Cmd+Z** (macOS) to step back.  

**Practice Exercise:**  
Create a small canvas (400 × 400 px). Paint a simple sun using a round brush (size ≈ 80 px, hardness ≈ 70 %). Then, switch to a soft brush (size ≈ 150 px, hardness ≈ 0 %) and add a subtle glow around the sun. This exercise demonstrates how size and hardness affect the feel of a stroke.

### Using the Eraser Tool  

The **Eraser** (shortcut **E**) works like a brush that paints with the **background color**—or, when you enable **“Use Brush”** mode, it behaves exactly like the Brush Tool but removes pixels instead of adding them.

1. **Select the Eraser** from the Tools Panel.  
2. **Choose a size & hardness** – The same shortcuts (`[` `]`) and Options Bar controls apply.  
3. **Erase** – Click‑drag over the area you want to clear. If you’re working on a **transparent layer**, the erased area becomes transparent (you’ll see the gray‑white checkerboard).  

> **Tip:** For precise erasing, switch the **Mode** in the Options Bar to **“Brush”** and turn on **“All Layers”** if you need to erase across multiple layers simultaneously.

---

## Crafting Your Own Brush Preset  

Photoshop ships with dozens of default brushes, but creating a custom brush lets you infuse your personal style into every project.

### Step‑by‑Step: Save a Custom Brush  

1. **Create the brush shape** –  
   * **Method A:** Use the **Brush Tool** with a unique size, hardness, and spacing.  
   * **Method B:** Convert any selection or shape into a brush. Draw a vector shape (e.g., a star) on a new layer, then go to **Edit → Define Brush**.  
2. **Open the Brush Settings panel** – Window → Brush Settings.  
3. **Fine‑tune** – Adjust **Shape Dynamics**, **Texture**, **Dual Brush**, or **Color Dynamics** to get the exact look you want.  
4. **Save the preset** – In the Brush Settings panel, click the **Create New Brush** icon (looks like a folded page) at the top right. A dialog appears:  
   * **Name** – Give it a descriptive name (e.g., “Soft Sunburst”).  
   * **Preset Manager** – Click **OK**. The new brush appears in the **Brush Preset Picker** (the dropdown next to the Brush Tool icon).  
5. **Organize** – Open **Window → Brush Presets**. You can drag your new brush into a custom group for easy access later.  

> **Tip:** If you plan to share the brush with others, select the brush in the preset picker, then click the **Export Selected Brushes** button (the little folder icon) to save a **.abr** file.

### Quick Checklist for a Good Custom Brush  

- **Consistent size** – Ensure the brush tip size aligns with the intended use (e.g., fine detail vs. broad background).  
- **Balanced hardness** – Soft edges for natural media, hard edges for graphic work.  
- **Appropriate spacing** – Set to 1 % for smooth strokes; increase for stipple or scatter effects.  
- **Naming convention** – Include the intended use (e.g., “Watercolor‑Wash‑Large”) to locate it quickly later.

---

## Putting It All Together: Mini Project  

**Goal:** Add a hand‑drawn highlight to a portrait photo.  

1. **Open a portrait** (`File → Open`).  
2. **Create a new layer** (`Layer → New → Layer…`) so your brush work stays non‑destructive.  
3. **Pick a highlight color** – Use the **Eyedropper** to sample a bright spot on the subject’s cheek, then shift the hue slightly toward a warmer tone using the Color Picker.  
4. **Select a soft round brush** – Size ≈ 30 px, hardness ≈ 0 %, low spacing.  
5. **Paint the highlight** – Click‑drag over the cheek, building up the color gradually. Adjust **Opacity** in the Options Bar to keep the effect subtle.  
6. **Refine** – Switch to a smaller, harder brush (size ≈ 10 px, hardness ≈ 80 %) to add a crisp edge where the light catches.  
7. **Erase excess** – Use the Eraser with a soft edge (size ≈ 50 px, hardness ≈ 0 %) to blend the painted area into the skin.  
8. **Save a custom brush** – If you liked the shape of the highlight stroke, define it as a brush for future portraits.  

This workflow demonstrates how color selection, brush adjustments, and erasing combine to produce a polished, realistic effect—all while keeping the original photo untouched on its own layer.

---

## Frequently Asked Beginner Questions  

| Question | Answer |
|----------|--------|
| **Can I change the background color while using the Brush Tool?** | Yes. Click the background swatch (the hollow square) to open the Color Picker, then paint with tools that reference the background (e.g., Paint Bucket). |
| **Why does my brush sometimes look “jagged” even at a high size?** | Check the **Spacing** setting. A high spacing value creates visible gaps. Reduce it to ≤ 5 % for a smooth line. |
| **Do I need a graphics tablet to use Shape Dynamics?** | Not strictly. Without a tablet, you can still vary size or angle by using the **Pen Pressure** option set to **“Off”** and manually adjusting the **Size Jitter** slider. |
| **What’s the difference between Opacity and Flow?** | Opacity limits the maximum transparency of each brush mark. Flow controls how quickly that opacity builds up as you drag. Think of Flow as “paint application speed.” |
| **Can I delete a custom brush I no longer need?** | Open the **Brush Presets** panel, right‑click the brush, and choose **Delete Brush**. Confirm the deletion. |

---

## Tips for Building Good Brush Habits  

- **Use keyboard shortcuts** (`[` `]` for size, **Shift+[`]** for hardness) to keep your flow uninterrupted.  
- **Preview brush changes** – In the Brush Settings panel, the preview window shows a live representation of your adjustments.  
- **Keep a “Color Reference” layer** – Duplicate a small portion of your image, lock the layer, and use it as a visual guide for consistent hue selection.  
- **Name layers descriptively** – When you start painting on a new layer, rename it (e.g., “Sun Highlights”) to stay organized, especially as you add multiple brush elements later.  

---

## ## Key Takeaways  

- **Foreground vs. background colors** are set via the swatches; the foreground is what the Brush and Eraser tools paint with.  
- **Three primary color selection methods**: Color Picker (precise hue), Swatches panel (quick access to saved colors), and Eyedropper tool (sample directly from the canvas).  
- **Brush Settings panel** gives deep control over size, hardness, spacing, and advanced dynamics; the Options Bar handles quick changes to size, hardness, opacity, and flow.  
- **Painting strokes**: Adjust size/hardness, use `[ ]` shortcuts, and practice with simple shapes to feel the impact of each setting.  
- **Eraser tool** works like a brush that removes pixels; its size and hardness behave the same as a regular brush.  
- **Saving a custom brush**: Define a shape, tweak settings, click the “new brush” icon, name it, and optionally group it for future projects.  
- **Non‑destructive workflow**: Always paint on a new layer so you can edit, erase, or hide brush work without affecting the original image.  

You now have the foundational tools to choose colors confidently, manipulate brush behavior, and preserve your custom brush creations for any future Photoshop project. Happy painting!

modules.title: 4. Basic Photo Editing: Cropping, Resizing, and Adjustments
modules.content:
## 1. A Real‑World Problem: The “Perfect” Instagram Post  

You’ve just captured a vibrant street‑scene on your phone. The composition looks great, but the horizon is a little crooked, the edges contain distracting clutter, and the image is larger than the 1080 × 1080 px square you need for Instagram.  

What do you do?  
You could re‑shoot the photo, but with Photoshop you can **crop** the unwanted area, **straighten** the horizon, **resize** the canvas to the exact dimensions your platform requires, and make a quick **brightness/contrast** tweak—all in a few minutes.  

The steps below walk you through exactly that workflow, showing how the same techniques apply to any photo you need to polish.

---

## 2. Cropping & Straightening the Image  

### 2.1 What the Crop Tool Does  

The **Crop tool** (shortcut **C**) lets you trim away pixels outside a defined rectangle. While cropping, Photoshop also offers a **Straighten** option: you draw a line along a reference edge (e.g., a building’s roof), and Photoshop rotates the image so that line becomes perfectly horizontal or vertical.

> **Tip:** The Crop tool works on the **current layer**. If you have multiple layers, make sure the layer you want to edit is selected in the **Layers panel** (introduced in Chapter 2).

### 2.2 Step‑by‑Step: Cropping a Photo  

1. **Select the Crop tool** from the Tools panel or press **C**.  
2. In the **Options Bar** (just below the Menu Bar), you’ll see fields for **Width**, **Height**, and **Resolution**.  
   - For a square Instagram post, type `1080 px` for both Width and Height.  
   - Leave **Resolution** blank unless you’re preparing the file for print (300 ppi is standard for print).  
3. Click anywhere on the image. A rectangular marquee appears, surrounded by **handles** at the corners and mid‑sides.  
4. **Drag the handles** to include the portion you want to keep.  
   - As you move the edges, Photoshop shows a live preview of the cropped result.  
5. To **straighten** the horizon:  
   - Hover just outside a corner handle until the cursor turns into a **rotate** icon.  
   - Click and drag to rotate the crop box, or—more precisely—click the **Straighten** button (a small ruler icon) in the Options Bar.  
   - Draw a line along the horizon or any edge that should be level. Photoshop will automatically rotate the image so that line becomes horizontal.  
6. Press **Enter** (or click the check‑mark in the Options Bar) to apply the crop.  

> **Note:** Cropping **deletes** the trimmed pixels from the file, but Photoshop keeps a **non‑destructive copy** in the **History panel** (see Section 5). You can always revert if needed.

### 2.3 Common Cropping Scenarios  

| Scenario | Recommended Settings |
|----------|----------------------|
| Social‑media square (Instagram, Facebook) | Width = Height = 1080 px (or 1200 px for higher quality) |
| Landscape banner for a website | Set only **Width** or **Height** and leave the other blank to maintain aspect ratio |
| Print‑ready photo (4 × 6 in) | Width = 4 in, Height = 6 in, Resolution = 300 ppi |

---

## 3. Resizing Images: Image Size vs. Canvas Size  

Photos often need to be adjusted **after** cropping. Photoshop offers two distinct commands:

| Command | What it changes | Typical use |
|---------|----------------|-------------|
| **Image > Image Size** | Alters the **pixel dimensions** (and optionally the resolution) of the **entire image**. This resamples the picture, adding or removing pixel data. | Preparing files for print, reducing file size for web, or enlarging a small image (with caution). |
| **Image > Canvas Size** | Expands or shrinks the **canvas**—the outer boundary that holds your layers—without altering the existing pixels. New canvas area is filled with a background color or left transparent. | Adding a border, creating space for text, or matching a specific document size. |

### 3.1 Using Image Size  

1. Choose **Image > Image Size** from the Menu Bar.  
2. The **Image Size dialog** appears with three key fields: **Width**, **Height**, and **Resolution**.  
3. Decide whether you want to **constrain proportions** (the chain link icon). For most cases, keep it on so Photoshop maintains the aspect ratio.  
4. Enter the new dimensions:  
   - To **downsize** a 4000 × 3000 px photo to 1200 × 900 px, type `1200` for Width. Height updates automatically.  
   - To **upsize** carefully, check the **Resample** dropdown. Choose **Preserve Details 2.0** (or **Bicubic Smoother**) for enlargement; this algorithm attempts to keep edges sharp.  
5. Click **OK**.  

> **Caution:** Upscaling beyond 200 % often produces soft or blurry results. If you need a large print, consider using a dedicated up‑scaling tool or a vector‑based approach.

### 3.2 Using Canvas Size  

1. Open **Image > Canvas Size**.  
2. The dialog shows the current canvas dimensions.  
3. To **add a 50‑pixel white border** around the image:  
   - Increase both Width and Height by 100 px (50 px on each side).  
   - Choose **Relative** to enter the amount you want to add rather than the final size.  
   - Set the **Anchor** grid to the center (default) so the extra space is added equally on all sides.  
   - Pick a **Canvas extension color** (white, black, or a custom color). If your document has transparent background, select **Transparent**.  
4. Click **OK**.  

Canvas Size is especially useful when you need to match a **layout grid** (e.g., a brochure template) without altering the photo itself.

---

## 4. Quick Tonal Adjustments  

After cropping and resizing, the image may still need a little **tonal correction**—adjusting how light or dark the picture appears. Photoshop supplies several simple, one‑click adjustments that work directly on the **current layer**.

### 4.1 Brightness / Contrast  

1. With the layer selected, go to **Image > Adjustments > Brightness/Contrast**.  
2. In the dialog:  
   - **Brightness** slides the whole tonal range up (lighter) or down (darker).  
   - **Contrast** expands or compresses the difference between light and dark areas.  
3. Move the sliders while watching the preview.  
4. Click **OK** when satisfied.  

> **Tip:** A small increase in contrast (≈ +10) often makes a flat image pop, but avoid pushing it too far—details can disappear in shadows or highlights.

### 4.2 Exposure  

The **Exposure** command works like the exposure knob on a camera: it lifts or lowers the overall light level while preserving highlight and shadow detail.

1. Choose **Image > Adjustments > Exposure**.  
2. Adjust the **Exposure** slider (increments of 0.1). Positive values brighten; negative values darken.  
3. The **Offset** slider adds a uniform value to every pixel, useful for correcting a slight color cast.  
4. Click **OK**.  

### 4.3 Levels  

**Levels** gives you fine‑grained control over shadows, midtones, and highlights.

1. Open **Image > Adjustments > Levels**.  
2. The histogram shows the distribution of tones. Three draggable triangles sit below it:  

   - **Left triangle (black point)** – moves the darkest pixels up, deepening shadows.  
   - **Middle triangle (midtone)** – slides the overall brightness.  
   - **Right triangle (white point)** – pushes the brightest pixels higher, brightening highlights.  

3. Click on a triangle and drag left or right while watching the image update.  
4. For a quick fix, click the **Auto** button; Photoshop automatically sets the black and white points based on the histogram.  

> **Pro tip:** Hold **Shift** while dragging a triangle to constrain its movement, ensuring you don’t accidentally clip important detail.

### 4.4 When to Use Which Adjustment  

| Adjustment | Best For | Typical Settings |
|------------|----------|------------------|
| **Brightness / Contrast** | Quick overall lift or flattening | +10 Contrast, ±5 Brightness |
| **Exposure** | Correcting a mis‑exposed shot (e.g., underexposed) | +0.3 Exposure for a dark image |
| **Levels** | Fine‑tuning shadows and highlights, correcting color casts | Drag black point to the leftmost pixel that should be pure black; white point to the rightmost pixel that should be pure white |

All three adjustments are **destructive** when applied directly (they alter pixel values). In later chapters you’ll learn **Adjustment Layers** for non‑destructive edits, but for quick fixes on a single‑layer file, these commands are perfect.

---

## 5. Undo, Redo, and Snapshot History  

Even seasoned editors make mistakes. Photoshop’s **History panel** (found under **Window > History**) records every step you take, letting you move back and forth instantly.

### 5.1 Basic Undo / Redo  

- **Undo**: Press **Ctrl + Z** (Windows) or **Cmd + Z** (Mac). Photoshop toggles between the last two states.  
- **Step Backward**: **Ctrl + Alt + Z** (Windows) / **Cmd + Option + Z** (Mac) moves one step further back in the history list.  
- **Step Forward**: **Ctrl + Shift + Z** (Windows) / **Cmd + Shift + Z** (Mac) moves forward.  

> **Note:** The History panel lets you see the full list of actions, not just the last two.

### 5.2 Using the History Panel  

1. Open the panel via **Window > History**.  
2. Each entry is labeled (e.g., “Crop”, “Image Size”, “Brightness/Contrast”).  
3. Click any entry to **revert** the document to that state. All subsequent steps disappear from the list (they’re not deleted; you can redo them by moving forward again).  

### 5.3 Snapshots: Bookmarking a Moment  

A **snapshot** is a manual “bookmark” you can create at any point. It’s especially handy before making a big change, such as applying a dramatic exposure shift.

1. In the History panel, click the **camera icon** at the bottom to create a **snapshot**.  
2. Name it (e.g., “Before exposure tweak”).  
3. Continue editing.  
4. To compare, click the snapshot name; Photoshop shows the image as it was at that moment, while the current state remains visible in the main canvas.  

Snapshots are **non‑linear**: you can jump between them without losing the steps that follow the snapshot. They act like a personal “undo checkpoint”.

> **Pro tip:** Take a snapshot before any **destructive adjustment** (Brightness/Contrast, Levels, etc.). This gives you a safety net in case you need to revert to the original tonal balance.

---

## 6. Putting It All Together: A Guided Walkthrough  

Let’s apply everything to a sample image, “city‑street.jpg”.

1. **Open the file** (`File > Open`).  
2. **Crop to a square**:  
   - Select the Crop tool (**C**).  
   - Set Width = Height = 1080 px in the Options Bar.  
   - Draw the crop box around the central building.  
   - Click the **Straighten** button, draw a line along the building’s roof.  
   - Press **Enter**.  
3. **Resize for web**:  
   - Choose **Image > Image Size**.  
   - Confirm dimensions are still 1080 × 1080 px (Photoshop may have already set that).  
   - Set **Resolution** to 72 ppi (standard web).  
   - Click **OK**.  
4. **Create a snapshot**: “After crop”. Click the camera icon in History.  
5. **Adjust brightness**:  
   - `Image > Adjustments > Brightness/Contrast`.  
   - Increase Brightness to **+15**, Contrast to **+10**.  
   - Click **OK**.  
6. **Fine‑tune with Levels**:  
   - `Image > Adjustments > Levels`.  
   - Drag the black point to the leftmost visible shadow, white point to the rightmost highlight.  
   - Click **OK**.  
7. **Undo a mistake**: Accidentally increased Contrast too much.  
   - Press **Ctrl + Alt + Z** (Step Backward) until the previous Levels dialog is reached.  
   - Adjust the contrast slider to **+5** instead of **+10**.  
8. **Save for Instagram**:  
   - `File > Export > Save for Web (Legacy)…` (covered later).  
   - Choose **JPEG**, Quality **80**, and click **Save**.  

At any point you could click the “After crop” snapshot to compare the original composition with the final, edited version.

---

## 7. Frequently Asked Questions  

**Q1. Will cropping permanently delete the pixels I cut out?**  
Yes, the trimmed pixels are removed from the file. However, because Photoshop records each step in the History panel, you can revert to the pre‑crop state as long as you haven’t closed the document.

**Q2. Should I always resize images to the exact pixel dimensions required for the web?**  
Resizing to the target dimensions **before** exporting reduces file size and speeds up loading. If you need multiple sizes (e.g., thumbnail and full‑size), create copies of the file or use **Export > Export As** later.

**Q3. How can I tell if I’m losing quality when I upscale an image?**  
Zoom in to **100 %** (actual pixel view). If edges appear blurry or pixelated, the upscaling algorithm couldn’t create new detail. Consider using **Preserve Details 2.0** or a dedicated AI upscaler.

**Q4. What’s the difference between “undo” and “step backward”?**  
Undo (**Ctrl + Z**) toggles between the last two states. Step backward moves further back through the entire history list, allowing you to revert multiple steps.

**Q5. Can I crop without affecting the underlying layers?**  
The Crop tool works on the **active layer**. If you need to preserve other layers, either lock them before cropping or duplicate the layer you wish to crop and work on the copy.

---

## 8. Best Practices for Efficient Photo Editing  

- **Plan the final size first.** Knowing whether the image will be used for print or web helps you choose the right resolution early, avoiding unnecessary resampling.  
- **Crop before you resize.** Removing unwanted areas reduces the pixel count, making subsequent resizing faster and often yielding sharper results.  
- **Use snapshots before major tonal changes.** This gives you a quick way to compare “before” and “after” without creating separate files.  
- **Keep an eye on the histogram.** While you won’t see it often in these simple adjustments, a balanced histogram (no clipping at either end) usually indicates a well‑exposed image.  
- **Leverage the History panel as a workspace.** Treat each entry like a step in a recipe; you can jump back, reorder, or even branch off into a new edit sequence.

---

## Key Takeaways  

- The **Crop tool** lets you trim and straighten images; set exact dimensions in the Options Bar for platform‑specific output.  
- **Image Size** changes pixel dimensions (and resolution) of the entire picture, while **Canvas Size** expands or contracts the surrounding workspace without altering existing pixels.  
- Quick tonal fixes—**Brightness/Contrast**, **Exposure**, and **Levels**—are accessible via **Image > Adjustments** and work directly on the selected layer.  
- **Undo (Ctrl/Cmd + Z)** toggles the last action; **Step Backward/Forward** and the **History panel** provide full navigation through your edit trail.  
- **Snapshots** act as manual checkpoints, enabling instant comparison and safe experimentation before irreversible changes.  

By mastering these foundational tools, you now have a reliable workflow for cleaning up, resizing, and brightening any photo—ready for social media, web, or print.

modules.title: 5. Introduction to Masks & Transparency
modules.content:
## Seeing Through Layers: Why Transparency Matters  

Imagine you’ve just taken a beautiful portrait, but the background is a busy street that steals the focus from the subject. You could **crop** the image, but that would cut off parts of the person’s shoulders. Instead, you can **hide** the unwanted background while keeping the original pixels intact—so you can bring the street back later if you change your mind. This is the power of **layer transparency** and **masks**.  

Transparency lets you control **how much** of a layer shows through to the layers below it. By adjusting **Opacity** or using **Blend Modes**, you can make a layer partially visible, fully invisible, or anything in between. Masks take this a step further: they let you hide or reveal **specific areas** of a layer without erasing any data. Because the changes are non‑destructive, you can always tweak or reverse them later—an essential habit for any Photoshop beginner.

---

## Layer Transparency Basics  

### Opacity  

*Opacity* is the simplest way to make a whole layer more or less visible.  

1. Select the layer you want to adjust in the **Layers panel**.  
2. Locate the **Opacity** slider at the top of the panel (just below the Blend Mode dropdown).  
3. Drag the slider left (decrease) or right (increase).  

- **100 %** = fully opaque (the default).  
- **0 %** = completely transparent (the layer disappears).  

Because you already saw how the **Opacity** slider works for brushes in *Chapter 3*, the same control applies to entire layers.  

### Blend Modes  

Blend Modes determine **how** a layer’s pixels combine with the pixels of layers beneath it. The most common modes for transparency work are:  

| Blend Mode | What It Does | Typical Use |
|------------|--------------|-------------|
| **Normal** | No special interaction; the layer sits on top. | Default; when you don’t need any blending. |
| **Multiply** | Darkens the underlying colors (like drawing with a black marker). | Adding shadows or darkening a background. |
| **Screen** | Lightens the underlying colors (like drawing with a white marker). | Brightening an image or creating a glow. |
| **Overlay** | Combines Multiply and Screen to increase contrast. | Adding texture or punchy color effects. |
| **Soft Light** | A gentler version of Overlay, adds subtle contrast. | Fine‑tuning lighting. |

To change a layer’s Blend Mode:  

1. Click the **Blend Mode** dropdown in the Layers panel.  
2. Hover over each option to see a live preview on your canvas.  

Understanding Blend Modes is useful when you later **combine masks with adjustment layers** (covered in later chapters), but even now they let you experiment with how a masked area interacts with the rest of the image.

---

## Introducing Layer Masks  

### What Is a Layer Mask?  

A **layer mask** is a grayscale thumbnail attached to a layer. It tells Photoshop **which parts of the layer to show** and **which parts to hide**:

- **White** on the mask = fully visible.  
- **Black** on the mask = completely hidden.  
- **Gray** (any shade between) = partially transparent, proportional to the gray value.  

Because the mask is a separate channel, the original layer content remains untouched. You can paint, erase, or modify the mask at any time, and the underlying image stays 100 % intact.

### Creating Your First Mask  

1. **Select a layer** you want to mask (e.g., a photo of a person).  
2. Click the **Add Layer Mask** button at the bottom of the Layers panel (it looks like a rectangle with a circle inside).  

   - A white thumbnail appears next to the layer’s thumbnail, indicating a **fully revealed** mask.  

3. **Zoom in** on the area you’ll work with (use the Zoom tool or press `Ctrl+`/`Cmd+` + `+`).  

### Painting with Black, White, and Gray  

Now you’ll learn the three fundamental “brush colors” for masks.

| Brush Color | Effect on Mask | Result on Layer |
|-------------|----------------|-----------------|
| **White**   | Paints white → reveals the layer. | The painted area becomes fully visible. |
| **Black**   | Paints black → hides the layer. | The painted area becomes invisible, showing whatever is below. |
| **Gray**    | Paints gray → partially transparent. | The painted area shows the layer at a reduced opacity (e.g., 50 % if you paint 50 % gray). |

**Step‑by‑step example:** Hide a cluttered background behind a portrait.

1. **Add a mask** to the portrait layer.  
2. Choose the **Brush tool** (`B`). In the **Options Bar**, set **Opacity** to 100 % and **Flow** to 100 % for solid strokes.  
3. **Set the foreground color** to **black** (press `D` then `X` to swap to black).  
4. **Paint over the background** you want to hide. As you paint, you’ll see the background disappear, revealing the layer(s) underneath (perhaps a plain color or a new background you’ll add later).  
5. If you accidentally erase too much, switch the foreground color to **white** and paint over the mistake to bring the original pixels back.  

**Using gray for subtle blending:**  

- Lower the brush **Opacity** to, say, **30 %**.  
- Paint with **black** on the mask’s edge. The reduced opacity creates a soft, feathered transition, useful for a natural‑looking cutout.  

### Quick Tips for Mask Painting  

- **Toggle mask visibility**: `Alt` + click (Windows) / `Option` + click (Mac) on the mask thumbnail to view the mask itself (white = visible, black = hidden).  
- **Disable the mask temporarily**: `Shift` + click the mask thumbnail. Photoshop will ignore the mask until you click again.  
- **Link/unlink** the mask from its layer: Click the chain icon between the layer thumbnail and the mask thumbnail. Unlinked masks let you move the mask independently of the layer content.  

---

## Quick Mask Mode: A Shortcut for Refined Selections  

### What Is Quick Mask?  

Quick Mask mode turns your **selection** into a **temporary mask** that you can edit with brushes, just like a layer mask. It’s especially handy when you need a **precise selection** that you’ll later convert into a mask.

### Activating Quick Mask  

1. Choose any **selection tool** (e.g., the **Lasso**, **Marquee**, or **Pen** tool).  
2. Click the **Quick Mask** button at the bottom of the Tools panel (a rectangle with a circle inside).  

   - The canvas now appears **red‑tinted** where the selection is **not** active. The red overlay represents the mask’s “hidden” area.  

### Editing the Quick Mask  

- **Brush with white** to add to the selection (removes the red overlay).  
- **Brush with black** to subtract from the selection (adds more red).  
- **Gray** creates a semi‑transparent edge, giving you a feathered selection.  

Because you already know how to control **Brush Opacity** and **Flow**, you can apply the same settings here for smooth edges.

### Exiting Quick Mask  

- Click the **Quick Mask** button again **or** press `Ctrl+Shift+I` (`Cmd+Shift+I` on Mac).  
- Photoshop converts the edited mask back into a **standard selection** (marching ants).  

Now you have a refined selection that you can:

- Fill with a color,  
- Apply a **Adjustment Layer**,  
- Or—most importantly for this chapter—**convert it into a layer mask**.

---

## Combining Masks with Selection Tools for Precise Edits  

### From Selection to Layer Mask  

1. **Create a selection** using any selection tool (e.g., draw a rough outline around a tree).  
2. **Refine the selection** (optional) with **Select → Modify → Feather** to soften edges.  
3. With the selection active, **click the Add Layer Mask** button.  

   - Photoshop instantly turns the selection into a mask: the selected area becomes **white** (visible) on the mask, and everything else turns **black** (hidden).  

### Editing the Mask After Creation  

Even after you’ve turned a selection into a mask, you can still paint on it:

- **Paint black** to hide more of the layer.  
- **Paint white** to reveal hidden parts.  
- **Use gray or low‑opacity brushes** for gradual transparency.  

### Practical Workflow: Isolating an Object  

Let’s walk through a realistic scenario—isolating a product photo from a cluttered studio backdrop.

1. **Open the image** and duplicate the background layer (`Ctrl+J`/`Cmd+J`). Work on the duplicate.  
2. **Select the object** with the **Quick Selection tool** (`W`). Roughly paint over the product.  
3. **Enter Quick Mask mode** (`Q`).  
4. **Refine edges**:  
   - Switch to a soft‑edged brush (`B`).  
   - Paint **white** on the mask where the selection missed fine details (e.g., the product’s edge).  
   - Paint **black** where the selection included unwanted background.  
5. **Exit Quick Mask** (`Q`). The refined selection now appears as marching ants.  
6. **Create a layer mask** by clicking the **Add Layer Mask** button.  
7. **Fine‑tune the mask**:  
   - Lower brush **Opacity** to 30 % and paint with **black** along the edge for a subtle feather.  
   - If you need to bring back a tiny spot, switch to **white** and paint it back.  

Now the product sits on its own transparent background, ready for a new backdrop or for export as a PNG with transparency.

### Using Selection Tools Directly on Masks  

You can also **apply selection tools to an existing mask**:

- **Alt/Option‑click** the mask thumbnail to view the mask.  
- Use the **Rectangular Marquee** or **Lasso** to select a portion of the mask.  
- Press `Delete` to fill the selected area with **black** (hide) or **white** (reveal).  

This technique is handy when you need to **clear a large rectangular area** of a mask quickly.

### Combining Multiple Masks  

Photoshop lets you **stack masks** by adding additional masks to the same layer (via **Layer → Layer Mask → Reveal All**). The masks are combined using **Multiply** logic: only the areas that are white in **all** masks stay visible.  

- **Scenario**: You have a portrait layer with a mask that hides the background, and you want to add a second mask that hides the subject’s hair for a special effect.  
- **Steps**:  
  1. Add the first mask (background).  
  2. Add a second mask (hair).  
  3. Paint black on the second mask where the hair should disappear.  

Because each mask works independently, you can toggle or delete them without affecting the other, preserving maximum flexibility.

---

## Hands‑On Exercise: Create a Transparent Composite  

> **Goal:** Combine two photos— a portrait and a scenic background—using masks and transparency.  

1. **Open both images** (`File → Open`).  
2. **Drag** the portrait layer onto the scenic background document (use the **Move tool**).  
3. **Arrange** the portrait layer above the background layer in the Layers panel.  
4. **Add a layer mask** to the portrait layer.  
5. **Paint black** on the mask to remove the portrait’s original background, revealing the scenic view behind.  
6. **Switch to Quick Mask mode** (`Q`).  
7. **Use a soft brush** to clean up any remaining stray pixels around the subject’s hair.  
8. **Exit Quick Mask** (`Q`).  
9. **Adjust the portrait layer’s Opacity** to 90 % for a subtle blend with the scenery.  
10. **Experiment with Blend Modes** (e.g., **Overlay** or **Soft Light**) to see how the portrait integrates with the background.  

When you’re satisfied, **save** the file as a PSD (`File → Save As`) to preserve the masks, then export a PNG (`File → Export → Export As`) to keep the transparent background.

---

## Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them  

| Issue | Why It Happens | Quick Fix |
|-------|----------------|-----------|
| **Mask appears black (everything hidden)** | Accidentally painted the mask black or the mask thumbnail is linked to a hidden layer. | `Alt/Option`‑click the mask thumbnail to view it. Paint **white** where you want visibility. |
| **Brush strokes on mask look fuzzy** | Low **Brush Hardness** or low **Flow**. | Set **Hardness** to 100 % for crisp edges, or increase **Flow** if you need more solid strokes. |
| **Selection disappears after exiting Quick Mask** | You didn’t convert the Quick Mask to a selection before exiting. | Press `Ctrl+Enter` (`Cmd+Return`) to **load** the mask as a selection, then exit Quick Mask. |
| **Mask edges look harsh** | Painting with 100 % opacity on a mask creates a hard line. | Use a **soft‑edged brush** and lower **Opacity** (e.g., 30 %) to feather the edge. |
| **Layer disappears after adjusting Opacity** | The layer’s **Blend Mode** is set to something like **Multiply** on a dark background, making it look invisible. | Switch the Blend Mode back to **Normal** to see the layer’s true opacity. |

---

## Summary of Core Concepts  

- **Opacity** controls a layer’s overall transparency.  
- **Blend Modes** define how a layer’s pixels mathematically interact with those below.  
- **Layer masks** use grayscale information (black = hide, white = show, gray = partial) to hide or reveal parts of a layer **non‑destructively**.  
- **Quick Mask mode** lets you edit a selection as a temporary mask with brush tools, then turn it back into a standard selection.  
- **Combining masks with selections** gives you precise control: create a selection, convert it to a mask, then fine‑tune with brushes.  

Mastering these tools transforms you from a “pixel eraser” into a **non‑destructive editor**, a habit that will pay off throughout the rest of the book.

---

## Key Takeaways  

- **Opacity** and **Blend Modes** affect an entire layer’s visibility; masks let you target specific areas.  
- **White on a mask = fully visible**, **black = fully hidden**, **gray = partial transparency**.  
- **Create a mask** by clicking the **Add Layer Mask** button; paint with black, white, or gray to control visibility.  
- **Quick Mask mode** (shortcut `Q`) turns a selection into a temporary mask you can edit with brushes; exit with `Q` to restore the selection.  
- **Convert selections to masks** for precise, non‑destructive edits, and refine them with brush tools or additional selection commands.  
- Non‑destructive workflow = **always keep the original pixels**, allowing you to revisit and revise any edit later.

modules.title: 6. Text & Shape Tools
modules.content:
## Adding Text: Point, Area, and Paragraph

### Picking the Right Text Tool  
The **Type Tool** lives in the Tools Panel (look for the “T” icon). Click it once to reveal three sub‑options in the **Options Bar**:

| Option | When to use it |
|--------|----------------|
| **Point Text** | You need a single line or a short burst of text that expands as you type. |
| **Area Text** | You want text to flow inside a rectangular or elliptical container—ideal for captions or blocks of copy. |
| **Paragraph Text** | Same as Area Text, but the container automatically expands vertically to fit the whole paragraph. |

> **Tip:** If you’re unsure, start with Point Text; you can always convert it later (see the **Convert to Paragraph Text** button in the Options Bar).

### Point Text – The Quick‑Start Method  
1. **Select the Type Tool** (T).  
2. **Click anywhere** on the canvas. A blinking cursor appears.  
3. **Start typing**. As you type, the box grows horizontally.  
4. **Press Enter/Return** to start a new line; the box will keep expanding.  

Because Point Text is anchored to a single point, you can move the whole block by selecting the **Move Tool** (V) and dragging the text layer.

### Area Text – Controlling the Layout  
1. **Select the Type Tool** and click‑and‑drag to draw a rectangle (or ellipse, if you’re using the **Elliptical Marquee** while the tool is active).  
2. Release the mouse. A **text box** appears inside the shape.  
3. **Type or paste** your content. Text will automatically wrap to the next line when it reaches the edge of the box.  

**Why use Area Text?** It lets you set a fixed width, which is essential for columns, captions, or any design where line length matters.

### Paragraph Text – Let the Box Grow With You  
1. **Select the Type Tool** and double‑click anywhere on the canvas.  
2. Photoshop creates a **Paragraph Text layer** that expands vertically as you type.  

> **Note:** Paragraph Text behaves like Area Text with an “auto‑height” container. It’s perfect for longer copy where you don’t want to worry about manually resizing the box.

### Modifying Font Properties  
All font‑related settings live in the **Options Bar** when the Type Tool is active, and you can also open the **Character** and **Paragraph** panels (Window → Character / Paragraph).

| Property | Where to find it | What it does |
|----------|-------------------|--------------|
| **Font Family** | Options Bar drop‑down | Chooses the typeface (e.g., *Arial*, *Helvetica*). |
| **Style** | Options Bar (Regular, Bold, Italic…) | Applies weight or slant. |
| **Size** | Options Bar (numeric field) | Controls the height of the letters. |
| **Color** | Swatch box in Options Bar | Sets the fill color of the text. |
| **Leading** | Character panel (line‑spacing) | Determines the vertical distance between lines. |
| **Tracking** | Character panel (letter‑spacing) | Adjusts space between all characters uniformly. |
| **Kerning** | Character panel (pair‑spacing) | Fine‑tunes space between specific character pairs. |
| **Alignment** | Paragraph panel (left, center, right, justify) | Aligns lines within the text box. |
| **Opacity** | Options Bar (same slider used for layers) | Makes the whole text layer more transparent. |
| **Blend Mode** | Options Bar (next to Opacity) | Defines how the text interacts with layers beneath it. |

**Quick workflow:**  
- Click the text layer in the **Layers Panel** to activate it.  
- Adjust the font, size, and color in the Options Bar.  
- Open the **Character panel** for leading, tracking, and kerning.  
- Open the **Paragraph panel** for alignment and justification.  

All changes are **non‑destructive**: you can revisit any property later without re‑typing.

---

## Working with Vector Shapes

### Shape Tools Overview  
Photoshop’s **Shape Tools** create **vector** objects—mathematically defined paths that stay crisp at any size. The three primary shape tools are:

| Tool | Icon | Typical Use |
|------|------|--------------|
| **Rectangle Tool** | ▭ | Boxes, buttons, UI elements |
| **Ellipse Tool** | ◯ | Circles, bubbles, decorative ovals |
| **Custom Shape Tool** | ★ | Stars, arrows, logos (pre‑made vectors) |

All shape tools share the same **Options Bar**, where you can toggle **Fill**, **Stroke**, and **Shape Mode** (Shape, Path, Pixels).

### Drawing a Rectangle  
1. **Select the Rectangle Tool** (U).  
2. In the **Options Bar**, set **Fill** to a color (or **No Fill** if you only want a stroke) and **Stroke** to a contrasting color.  
3. **Click‑and‑drag** on the canvas. Hold **Shift** while dragging to constrain the shape to a perfect square.  
4. Release the mouse. A new **shape layer** appears in the Layers Panel.

### Drawing an Ellipse  
1. Choose the **Ellipse Tool** (U).  
2. Set Fill and Stroke as desired.  
3. **Click‑and‑drag**. Hold **Shift** for a perfect circle, **Alt/Option** to draw from the center outward.  

### Using the Custom Shape Tool  
1. Click the **Custom Shape Tool** (U) and open the **Shape picker** in the Options Bar.  
2. Click the **gear icon** → **Shapes** → **All** to load the full library.  
3. Select a shape (e.g., a star).  
4. **Click‑and‑drag** to place it. Hold **Shift** to keep the aspect ratio.  

> **Tip:** You can import your own SVG files (File → Place Embedded) and Photoshop will treat them as vector shape layers.

### Editing Paths – The Vector Toolbox  
After a shape is placed, you can refine its geometry:

| Tool | Icon | What it does |
|------|------|--------------|
| **Path Selection Tool** (A) | Black arrow | Moves the entire shape. |
| **Direct Selection Tool** (A) | White arrow | Selects individual anchor points for precise adjustments. |
| **Add Anchor Point** (found under the Pen Tool) | + | Inserts new points along the path. |
| **Delete Anchor Point** | – | Removes points, simplifying the shape. |
| **Convert Point Tool** | ↔︎ | Changes a corner point to a smooth curve (or vice‑versa). |

**Example – Tweaking a Custom Star:**  
1. Choose the **Direct Selection Tool**.  
2. Click a corner point; a small **bounding box** appears.  
3. Drag the point inward to shorten a spike, or hold **Shift** while dragging to keep the motion constrained to the axis.  

### Adding Fill, Stroke, and Basic Layer Styles  
- **Fill** determines the interior color.  
- **Stroke** outlines the shape; its thickness is set in the Options Bar (numeric field).  

To add a **layer style** (e.g., Drop Shadow) to a shape:  

1. Double‑click the shape layer (not the thumbnail) in the **Layers Panel** to open the **Layer Style** dialog.  
2. Check **Drop Shadow**, **Inner Glow**, or any other effect you need.  
3. Adjust the sliders; you’ll see the changes live on the canvas.  

> **Remember:** Layer styles are also **non‑destructive** and can be toggled on/off at any time.

---

## Converting Shapes to Smart Objects

### Why Convert?  
A **Smart Object** stores the original vector data inside a layer. This gives you two major advantages:

1. **Scalable editing** – Resize the shape without losing crispness.  
2. **Non‑destructive filters** – Apply filters (e.g., Blur, Distort) that can be edited or removed later.

### Converting a Shape Layer  
1. Right‑click the shape layer in the **Layers Panel**.  
2. Choose **Convert to Smart Object**.  
3. The layer thumbnail now shows a small **smart‑object icon** (a little page).  

### Editing the Smart Object Later  
1. Double‑click the smart‑object thumbnail. Photoshop opens the vector shape in a **new document window**.  
2. Make any changes (adjust anchor points, change fill color, add new shapes).  
3. **Save** (Ctrl/Cmd + S) and close the window. Your original composition updates instantly.  

> **Pro tip:** Keep the original shape layer **hidden** (click the eye icon) if you want to compare before/after versions while you experiment.

---

## Practical Scenario: Designing a Simple Logo

Imagine you need a clean logo for a coffee shop called **“Brewed Awakenings.”** The brief calls for:

- The word “Brewed” in a bold, modern sans‑serif.  
- The word “Awakenings” in a lighter script beneath it.  
- A circular emblem containing a coffee bean icon.

### Step‑by‑Step

1. **Create a new document** (File → New) sized 1200 × 1200 px, 300 dpi – perfect for both web and print.  
2. **Add the main text**:  
   - Select the **Type Tool**, click the canvas, and type **BREWED**.  
   - In the Options Bar, set **Font** to *Montserrat Bold*, **Size** to 150 pt, **Color** to a deep brown (`#4B2E2A`).  
3. **Add the tagline**:  
   - Switch to **Paragraph Text**, click below the first word, and type **Awakenings**.  
   - Choose *Great Vibes* (a script font), **Size** 80 pt, **Color** `#8C6E58`.  
   - Use the **Paragraph panel** to center‑align both lines.  
4. **Create the circular emblem**:  
   - Choose the **Ellipse Tool**, set **Fill** to `#FFF` (white), **Stroke** to `#4B2E2A`, thickness 5 px.  
   - Hold **Shift** while dragging to make a perfect circle, then position it above the text using the **Move Tool**.  
5. **Insert a coffee bean icon**:  
   - Use **File → Place Embedded**, locate a simple SVG coffee bean, and click **Place**.  
   - The SVG appears as a **shape layer**. Resize (`Ctrl/Cmd + T`) while holding **Shift** to keep proportions.  
   - Center the bean inside the circle.  
6. **Apply a subtle Drop Shadow** to the circle:  
   - Double‑click the circle layer → **Drop Shadow**.  
   - Set **Opacity** 30 %, **Distance** 5 px, **Size** 8 px, angle 120°.  
7. **Convert the emblem to a Smart Object**:
