   - Select both the circle and bean layers (`Shift`‑click), right‑click, **Convert to Smart Object**.  
   - Now you can scale the whole emblem up or down without losing crispness.  
8. **Final adjustments**:  
   - Group the text layers (`Ctrl/Cmd + G`) and name the group **Logo Text**.  
   - Lower the **Opacity** of the tagline to 85 % for a softer look.  

You now have a fully editable logo, ready for export (the next chapter will cover that).

---

## Tips & Common Pitfalls

- **Accidental rasterization:** If you click **Rasterize** on a shape layer, you lose the vector data. Undo (`Ctrl/Cmd + Z`) immediately or keep a backup copy.  
- **Stroke alignment:** By default, strokes are centered on the path edge. Use the **Shape Options** (Window → Properties) to shift the stroke **Inside** or **Outside** for cleaner edges.  
- **Text overflow:** When using Area Text, you’ll see a red plus sign (+) at the bottom of the box—this indicates the text exceeds the container. Resize the box or reduce the font size.  
- **Smart Object limitations:** Certain filters (e.g., **Liquify**) cannot be applied directly to a Smart Object; you must rasterize first, which defeats the purpose. Plan your workflow accordingly.  
- **Performance tip:** Turning off **Layer Visibility** for layers you’re not editing (click the eye icon) speeds up the canvas redraw, especially when working with many shapes and text layers.

---

## Key Takeaways

- **Three text modes**—Point, Area, Paragraph—serve different layout needs; all can be edited via the Options Bar, Character, and Paragraph panels.  
- **Shape Tools** (Rectangle, Ellipse, Custom Shape) create vector layers that stay crisp at any size; you can edit their paths with the Direct Selection and Path tools.  
- **Fill, Stroke, and basic Layer Styles** (e.g., Drop Shadow) give immediate visual polish while remaining non‑destructive.  
- **Converting shapes to Smart Objects** preserves vector fidelity and lets you apply editable filters later.  
- A **structured workflow**—type → shape → style → smart‑object conversion—keeps your composition organized and flexible for future tweaks.

modules.title: 7. Simple Photo Effects: Filters & Adjustment Layers
modules.content:
## Adding Adjustment Layers for Creative Control  

Photoshop’s **adjustment layers** let you change the look of an image without permanently altering the original pixels. Because they sit above your photo layer, you can turn them on or off, change their order, or edit their settings at any time—exactly the kind of non‑destructive workflow you practiced with masks in Chapter 5.  

### Why Use Adjustment Layers?  

- **Safety:** The underlying image stays untouched. If you don’t like the result, simply delete the adjustment layer.  
- **Flexibility:** Multiple adjustments can be stacked, each with its own opacity and blend mode.  
- **Reusability:** Drag an adjustment layer onto another document to reuse the same settings.  

### Where to Find the Adjustment Layer Buttons  

The **Layers panel** (introduced in Chapter 2) contains a row of icons at its bottom. The first icon looks like a half‑filled circle; clicking it opens the **New Adjustment Layer** menu. From there you can choose **Hue/Saturation**, **Color Balance**, **Levels**, and many more.

> **Tip:** If you prefer the menu bar, go to **Layer → New Adjustment Layer** and pick the same options.

### 1. Hue/Saturation  

**Hue/Saturation** lets you shift the overall color hue, boost or cut saturation (color intensity), and adjust lightness.  

1. Click the **New Adjustment Layer** icon and select **Hue/Saturation**.  
2. In the **Properties** panel that appears, you’ll see three sliders: **Hue**, **Saturation**, and **Lightness**.  
3. Drag the **Hue** slider left or right to rotate all colors around the color wheel.  
4. Move the **Saturation** slider to make colors more vivid (right) or more muted (left).  
5. Adjust **Lightness** to brighten or darken the entire image.  

**Practical scenario:** You’ve taken a portrait under midday sunlight, and the skin tones look a bit too warm. By lowering the **Hue** slightly and pulling back the **Saturation**, you can achieve a cooler, more natural look without ever touching the original photo layer.

### 2. Color Balance  

**Color Balance** gives you control over the mix of **Cyan‑Red**, **Magenta‑Green**, and **Yellow‑Blue** in the **shadows**, **midtones**, and **highlights**. This is especially handy for correcting color casts or creating a stylized mood.  

1. Choose **Color Balance** from the adjustment layer menu.  
2. In the **Properties** panel, you’ll see three sets of sliders labeled **Shadows**, **Midtones**, and **Highlights**.  
3. Pick a tonal range (e.g., **Midtones**) and slide the **Cyan‑Red** control toward **Red** if the image feels too cyan, or toward **Cyan** if it feels too red. Do the same for the other two color pairs.  
4. Use the **Preserve Luminosity** checkbox to keep the overall brightness stable while you shift colors.  

**Practical scenario:** A landscape photo taken at sunrise has a strong blue cast in the shadows. By moving the **Cyan‑Red** slider toward **Red** in the **Shadows** set, you can restore warmth without affecting the sky’s blue tones.

### 3. Levels  

**Levels** adjusts the tonal range by redefining the black point, white point, and midpoint (gamma). Think of it as a more precise version of the **Brightness/Contrast** adjustment you explored in Chapter 4.  

1. Select **Levels** from the New Adjustment Layer menu.  
2. The **Properties** panel shows a histogram with three draggable triangles: **black point** (left), **white point** (right), and **midpoint** (center).  
3. Drag the **black point** inward to deepen shadows, and drag the **white point** inward to brighten highlights.  
4. Move the **midpoint** left or right to make the image overall brighter or darker without clipping the extremes.  

**Practical scenario:** A backlit portrait looks flat because the camera couldn’t capture enough contrast. By pulling the black point slightly inward and the white point outward, you restore depth and make the subject pop.

### 4. Layer‑Specific Adjustments  

Adjustment layers affect every layer **below** them by default. If you want an adjustment to affect only a single layer (for example, just the background), you can **clip** the adjustment layer:  

1. Hover the adjustment layer in the Layers panel.  
2. Hold **Alt** (Windows) or **Option** (Mac) and click the line that appears between the adjustment layer and the layer beneath it.  
3. The adjustment layer will now have a small downward arrow indicating it’s clipped to the layer directly below.  

Clipping is a quick way to limit the effect without creating a mask.

---

## Applying Filters from the Filter Gallery  

Filters are algorithmic effects that transform pixels in a specific way—blur, sharpen, or add artistic styles. The **Filter Gallery** groups many of these effects under one window, letting you preview and combine them live.

### Opening the Filter Gallery  

1. Select the layer you want to affect (usually the photo layer).  
2. Choose **Filter → Filter Gallery** from the menu bar.  

A dialog appears with three columns: **Blur**, **Sharpen**, and **Artistic**. Each category contains a handful of preset filters.

### 1. Blur Filters  

- **Gaussian Blur:** Smooths the image uniformly, useful for softening skin or creating a dreamy background.  
- **Motion Blur:** Simulates movement in a single direction; set the angle and distance to match the intended motion.  

**How‑to use:** Drag the **Gaussian Blur** slider until the image looks soft, but keep an eye on the preview so you don’t lose too much detail.

### 2. Sharpen Filters  

- **Unsharp Mask:** Enhances edge contrast, making details appear crisper.  
- **Smart Sharpen:** Offers more control over shadow and highlight protection, reducing ringing artifacts.  

**How‑to use:** In **Unsharp Mask**, start with a low **Amount** (e.g., 50 %), a **Radius** of 1–2 px, and a **Threshold** of 0. Adjust until the image looks sharper but not oversharpened.

### 3. Artistic Filters  

- **Watercolor:** Turns the photo into a loose, paint‑like rendering.  
- **Poster Edges:** Creates a stylized, comic‑book look with bold outlines and flat colors.  

**How‑to use:** Choose **Poster Edges**, then tweak the **Edge Thickness**, **Edge Intensity**, and **Posterization** sliders to match the effect you envision.

### Previewing and Applying  

The preview pane updates in real time as you move sliders. You can also **stack** multiple filters by checking **Add to Existing Filters** (the little “plus” icon) before clicking **OK**. When you’re happy, click **OK** to apply the filter stack to the selected layer.

> **Tip:** If you accidentally apply a filter you don’t like, press **Ctrl + Z** (Windows) or **Cmd + Z** (Mac) to undo—it works just like undoing any other operation.

---

## Converting Filters to Smart Filters  

A **Smart Filter** is a filter that lives inside a **Smart Object** and remains editable. By converting a regular layer (or an entire filter stack) into a Smart Object before applying a filter, you gain the ability to tweak the filter later, adjust its opacity, or even change its blend mode—exactly the kind of non‑destructive flexibility you practiced with adjustment layers.

### 1. Turning a Layer into a Smart Object  

1. Select the layer you want to filter.  
2. Right‑click (or Control‑click) the layer thumbnail in the Layers panel and choose **Convert to Smart Object**.  

A small **smart object** icon appears on the layer thumbnail, indicating the layer now contains a reference to the original pixel data.

### 2. Applying a Filter as a Smart Filter  

With the Smart Object selected, go to **Filter → Filter Gallery** (or any other filter). Because the layer is a Smart Object, Photoshop automatically adds the filter as a **Smart Filter** underneath the layer in the Layers panel.  

- The filter appears indented under the Smart Object with a small **fx** icon.  
- Double‑clicking the filter opens its settings again, allowing you to fine‑tune the effect.  

### 3. Editing Smart Filters  

- **Adjust Settings:** Double‑click the filter name to reopen its dialog.  
- **Toggle Visibility:** Click the eye icon next to the filter to hide or show it without deleting it.  
- **Change Opacity:** Select the filter and use the **Opacity** slider at the top of the Layers panel (the same control you used for regular layers).  
- **Blend Mode:** With the filter selected, choose a blend mode (e.g., **Overlay**) from the dropdown to alter how the filter interacts with the underlying pixels.  

### 4. Stacking Multiple Smart Filters  

You can add as many Smart Filters as you like. Each one stacks in order, just like adjustment layers. To rearrange the order, simply drag a filter up or down within the Smart Object group.

**Practical scenario:** You want a portrait with a subtle **Gaussian Blur** on the background and a **Sharpness** boost on the eyes. Convert the photo layer to a Smart Object, apply a **Gaussian Blur** Smart Filter, then mask that filter (using the mask tools you learned in Chapter 5) so only the background is blurred. Next, add an **Unsharp Mask** Smart Filter and mask it so only the eyes remain sharpened. Because both are Smart Filters, you can later tweak the blur radius or the sharpening amount without starting over.

---

## Managing Visibility and Opacity of Adjustment Layers  

Just as you learned to toggle layer visibility with the eye icon, the same principle applies to adjustment layers. Adjustments can also be blended or faded using opacity.

### 1. Turning an Adjustment Layer On or Off  

- Click the **eye** icon next to the adjustment layer in the Layers panel.  
- When the eye is hidden, the adjustment’s effect disappears, letting you compare “before” and “after” instantly.  

### 2. Using Opacity to Fade an Effect  

- Select the adjustment layer.  
- Adjust the **Opacity** slider at the top of the Layers panel (or press **V** to activate the Move tool and then type a numeric opacity).  

A lower opacity creates a more subtle effect, which is handy when a full‑strength adjustment feels too aggressive.

### 3. Blend Modes for Adjustment Layers  

Adjustment layers also support **Blend Modes** (the same dropdown you used for regular layers). For example, setting a **Hue/Saturation** layer to **Color** blend mode will change only the hue and saturation while preserving the original luminance—perfect for recoloring objects without affecting shadows.

### 4. Grouping Adjustment Layers  

If you have several related adjustments (e.g., a **Hue/Saturation** followed by a **Levels** adjustment), you can **group** them:

1. Select the desired adjustment layers by holding **Shift** and clicking each.  
2. Press **Ctrl + G** (Windows) or **Cmd + G** (Mac) to create a group.  

Now you can hide, duplicate, or adjust the opacity of the entire group in one click, keeping your Layers panel tidy.

### 5. Quick Comparison Using the “Alt/Option” Click  

Holding **Alt** (Windows) or **Option** (Mac) while clicking the **eye** icon temporarily disables the layer (or group) while you keep the mouse button pressed. This lets you see the effect of the adjustment in real time without toggling the eye on and off repeatedly.

---

## Putting It All Together: A Mini Workflow  

Below is a concise step‑by‑step example that combines the techniques covered in this chapter. Imagine you have a **landscape photo** that needs a subtle color shift, a little extra contrast, and a dreamy blur on the sky.

1. **Create a Smart Object**  
   - Right‑click the photo layer → **Convert to Smart Object**.  

2. **Add a Color Balance Adjustment**  
   - Click the **New Adjustment Layer** icon → **Color Balance**.  
   - In the **Midtones**, slide **Cyan‑Red** a touch toward **Red** to warm the scene.  

3. **Add a Levels Adjustment**  
   - New Adjustment Layer → **Levels**.  
   - Drag the black point right a tiny amount and the white point left to boost contrast.  

4. **Apply a Sky Blur as a Smart Filter**  
   - With the Smart Object selected, go to **Filter → Filter Gallery** → **Blur → Gaussian Blur**.  
   - Set the radius to 8 px (enough to smooth clouds).  
   - Click **OK**.  

5. **Mask the Sky Blur**  
   - The Gaussian Blur Smart Filter automatically adds a mask.  
   - Select the mask thumbnail, then use the **Brush Tool** (set to white) to paint over the sky area, revealing the blur only there.  

6. **Fine‑Tune Opacity**  
   - Reduce the **Color Balance** layer’s opacity to 80 % for a more natural warmth.  
   - Lower the **Gaussian Blur** Smart Filter’s opacity to 60 % so the sky still retains some detail.  

7. **Toggle Visibility for Comparison**  
   - Click the eye icons on the adjustment layers and Smart Filter to see how each contributes to the final look.  

By the end of this workflow, you have a polished image where every change is reversible, perfectly illustrating the power of non‑destructive editing.

---

## Key Takeaways  

- **Adjustment layers** (Hue/Saturation, Color Balance, Levels) let you modify color and tonal attributes without altering original pixels.  
- **Filter Gallery** offers blur, sharpen, and artistic filters that can be previewed and stacked.  
- Converting a layer to a **Smart Object** before applying a filter creates a **Smart Filter**, which remains editable, maskable, and blend‑mode‑compatible.  
- Visibility (eye icon) and **Opacity** controls work on both adjustment layers and Smart Filters, enabling instant “before/after” comparisons and subtle effect blending.  
- Grouping, clipping, and masking adjustment layers give you precise control over where and how each effect is applied.  

With these tools, you can experiment freely, knowing every tweak is reversible—exactly the non‑destructive workflow that underpins professional Photoshop editing.

modules.title: 8. Exporting & Saving for Web & Print
modules.content:
### A Real‑World Situation: The Dual‑Purpose Project  

Imagine you’ve just finished designing a vibrant promotional banner for a client’s new product launch. The same design will appear in two places:

1. **Online** – as a header image on the company’s website, where fast loading speed and crisp colors on any screen are essential.  
2. **Print** – as a flyer that will be printed on a professional offset press and handed out at a trade show.

Both uses look like they should be the same file, but the technical requirements are completely different. One wrong setting and the web version could take forever to load, while the printed flyer might appear dull or blurry. This chapter shows you how to finish your Photoshop work so it shines on both the screen and the page.

---

## 1. Choosing the Right File Format  

A **file format** tells Photoshop (and any other program) how the image data is stored. The most common formats you’ll need as a beginner are:

| Format | Typical Use | Key Characteristics |
|--------|-------------|----------------------|
| **PSD** | Master file, future editing | Preserves **layers**, masks, adjustment layers, text, and all Photoshop settings. Large file size. |
| **JPEG** | Photographs on the web, email, quick‑share prints | lossy compression (some data discarded), adjustable **quality**, 8‑bit **RGB** only, no transparency. |
| **PNG** | Graphics with transparency, screenshots, UI elements | lossless compression (no quality loss), supports **alpha channel** (transparency), 8‑bit **RGB** or **RGBA**. |
| **GIF** | Simple animations, tiny icons, limited‑color graphics | 256‑color palette, lossless for those colors, supports simple **animation** and transparency. |

> **Tip:** Keep a **PSD** version of every project. It’s your “master copy” that lets you go back and change any layer, mask, or text later without starting from scratch.

### When to Use Each Format  

- **Web banner** → **JPEG** if the image is a full‑color photograph with no need for transparency, **PNG** if you need crisp edges or a transparent background, **GIF** only for very simple graphics or tiny animated loops.  
- **Print flyer** → **JPEG** at high quality (90‑100 % quality) *or* **PDF/TIFF** for professional printing (these aren’t covered in depth here, but the same principles apply).  

---

## 2. Resolution and Color Modes: 72 dpi vs 300 dpi, RGB vs CMYK  

### 2.1 What Is DPI?  

**DPI** stands for *dots per inch* and indicates how many pixels Photoshop will map to each inch when the image is rendered.  

- **72 dpi** – the historic screen standard. Modern monitors can display far more, but 72 dpi is still the default for most web‑export settings because it keeps file size low.  
- **300 dpi** – the typical requirement for high‑quality print. It gives the printer enough information to reproduce fine details without visible pixelation.

> **Important:** Changing DPI does **not** automatically change the pixel dimensions of your image. It only tells the output device how densely to place those pixels.

### 2.2 RGB vs CMYK  

- **RGB** (*Red, Green, Blue*) – the color mode used by screens. Each pixel is a combination of the three light colors. Most web formats (JPEG, PNG, GIF) support only RGB.  
- **CMYK** (*Cyan, Magenta, Yellow, Black*) – the color mode used by printers. Colors are created by subtracting light using ink. Converting an RGB image to CMYK can shift hues, especially bright blues and greens.

**When to switch color modes:**

- **Web work** – stay in **RGB**.  
- **Print work** – convert to **CMYK** *before* you export for print, using **Image → Mode → CMYK Color**.  

> **Tip:** Do a quick visual check after converting to CMYK. If colors look dull, you may need to adjust them with **Adjustment Layers** (which you already know how to add from Chapter 2).

---

## 3. Saving Your Master PSD  

Before you create any export, save a master copy that retains every editable element.

1. **File → Save As…** (or **Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + S**)  
2. Choose **Photoshop (*.PSD; *.PSB)** from the format dropdown.  
3. Pick a clear, descriptive filename (e.g., `ClientX_Banner_V1.psd`).  
4. Click **Save**.  

The PSD will keep:

- All **layers** (including those you built with the **Layers & Selections** tools).  
- **Masks** and **transparency** you created in Chapter 5.  
- Any **text** or **shape** objects from Chapter 6.  

Because PSD files are large, store them on a reliable drive or cloud folder. You’ll return to this file whenever the client asks for a color tweak or a new size.

---

## 4. Exporting for the Web  

Photoshop offers two primary ways to prepare images for online use:

1. **Export As** – the modern, streamlined dialog.  
2. **Save for Web (Legacy)** – the older dialog that still gives fine‑grained control over some settings.

Both achieve the same goal: a small file that still looks good on screen.

### 4.1 Using **Export As**  

1. **File → Export → Export As…** (or **Alt + Shift + Ctrl/Cmd + W**)  
2. The **Export As** panel appears on the right side of the workspace.  
3. **Select a format** from the dropdown (JPEG, PNG, GIF).  
4. Adjust **Image Size** if you need a smaller version (e.g., 800 × 600 px).  
5. Set **Resolution** to **72 dpi** for web.  
6. Use the **Quality** slider (for JPEG) or **Compression** (for PNG) to balance size and visual fidelity.  
7. Click the **Preview** button to see a side‑by‑side comparison of “Original” vs “Exported.”  
8. Choose a **Destination** folder and click **Export**.

#### Quick Export Settings Cheat Sheet  

| Goal | Format | Quality / Compression | When to Use |
|------|--------|-----------------------|-------------|
| Photo with many colors | JPEG | 60‑80 % (good balance) | Web banner, blog images |
| Transparent logo | PNG‑24 | No compression (lossless) | Icons, UI elements |
| Simple animation | GIF | 256‑color palette | Tiny animated ads |

### 4.2 Using **Save for Web (Legacy)**  

Some designers still prefer the older dialog because it offers **metadata** stripping and **color profile** options in one place.

1. **File → Export → Save for Web (Legacy)…**  
2. The **Save for Web** window opens with a preview pane.  
3. Choose a **preset** (e.g., **JPEG High**, **PNG‑24**, **GIF 128 Colors**) or start from **Custom**.  
4. **Adjust**:  
   - **Quality** (JPEG) or **Colors** (GIF).  
   - **Image Size** (percentage or exact pixel dimensions).  
   - **Dithering** (for PNG/GIF) – leave at default unless you need smoother gradients.  
5. **Metadata** dropdown – select **None** to strip EXIF data and reduce file size.  
6. **Convert to sRGB** – tick this box to ensure colors look consistent across browsers.  
7. The **optimized file size** appears at the bottom. Hover over the preview to see the exact kilobyte count.  
8. Click **Save**, name the file, and pick a folder.

> **Tip:** The **Preview** pane updates instantly as you move sliders, so you can experiment until the visual quality meets your expectations while staying under a target file size (e.g., < 150 KB for a banner).

### 4.3 Optimizing File Size Without Sacrificing Quality  

- **Resize first** – a 3000 × 2000 px image shrunk to 1200 × 800 px will automatically reduce file size.  
- **Use the right format** – a simple graphic with flat colors is usually smaller as PNG‑8 or GIF than as JPEG.  
- **Limit metadata** – EXIF data (camera info, GPS) isn’t needed for web assets.  
- **Check the “Convert to sRGB” box** – many browsers assume sRGB; using another profile can cause color shifts and larger files.

---

## 5. Exporting for Print  

Print files demand higher resolution, the correct color mode, and sometimes a different file type altogether. Here’s a straightforward workflow for a flat‑print piece like a flyer or poster.

### 5.1 Preparing the Document  

1. **Image → Image Size…**  
   - Set **Resolution** to **300 dpi**.  
   - Ensure **Resample** is **unchecked** if you only need to change the DPI without altering pixel dimensions.  
2. **Image → Mode → CMYK Color** (if the file is still in RGB).  
3. If your printer specifies a particular **color profile** (e.g., *U.S. Web Coated (SWOP) v2*), click **Edit → Assign Profile…** and choose the profile.  

> **Note:** Changing from RGB to CMYK can make some colors look less vibrant. Use **Adjustment Layers** (e.g., **Hue/Saturation**, **Selective Color**) to fine‑tune any problematic areas.

### 5.2 Exporting the Print‑Ready File  

While Photoshop’s **Export As** can produce a high‑quality JPEG, most professional printers prefer **PDF** or **TIFF** because they embed color profiles and support lossless compression. The steps are similar:

1. **File → Export → Export As…**  
2. Choose **JPEG** (or **TIFF** if you have the option) from the format list.  
3. Set **Resolution** to **300 dpi** (the dialog may show this automatically after you changed the document size).  
4. For JPEG, move the **Quality** slider to **90‑100 %** – this yields a large but still manageable file.  
5. Click **Export** and save with a clear name (e.g., `ClientX_Flyer_Print.jpg`).  

If your printer requests a PDF:

1. **File → Save As…**  
2. Choose **Photoshop PDF** from the format dropdown.  
3. In the **Save Adobe PDF** dialog, select **High Quality Print** preset.  
4. Verify that **CMYK** and the correct **color profile** are selected.  
5. Click **Save PDF**.

### 5.3 Quick Checklist for Print Export  

- **Resolution:** 300 dpi (or as specified).  
- **Color Mode:** CMYK (or keep RGB if the printer explicitly says so).  
- **Bleed:** Add 0.125 in (3 mm) extra on all sides if the design reaches the edge.  
- **File Format:** High‑quality JPEG, TIFF, or PDF.  
- **Embedded Profile:** Yes, unless told otherwise.  

---

## 6. A Simple Workflow from PSD to Final Assets  

Putting the pieces together, here’s a step‑by‑step routine you can follow for any project that needs both web and print outputs:

1. **Save the Master PSD** – always the first step after finishing the design.  
2. **Duplicate the PSD** (File → Duplicate) to create a *Web version* and a *Print version*; this prevents accidental changes to the original.  
3. **Web Version**  
   - Convert to **RGB** if not already.  
   - Set **Resolution** to **72 dpi**.  
   - Use **Export As** (or **Save for Web**) to generate JPEG/PNG/GIF files.  
   - Verify file size and visual quality using the preview pane.  
4. **Print Version**  
   - Convert to **CMYK**.  
   - Set **Resolution** to **300 dpi**.  
   - Add any required **bleed** (Canvas Size → Add).  
   - Export as high‑quality JPEG or PDF.  
5. **Organize Files**  
   - Create a folder structure such as `Project_Name / PSD / Web / Print`.  
   - Rename files clearly (`Banner_Web.jpg`, `Flyer_Print.pdf`).  

Following this routine ensures you never lose a layer, never forget to change a color mode, and always deliver the right file for the right medium.

---

## 7. Common Beginner Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them  

| Pitfall | Why It Happens | Fix |
|---------|----------------|-----|
| **Saving a web image as a PSD** | Forgetting to export after working in the master file. | Always **Export As** after the final edit; keep the PSD untouched. |
| **Leaving the image at 72 dpi for print** | Assuming “pixel dimensions” are enough. | Change **Resolution** to **300 dpi** before exporting for print. |
| **Exporting a PNG with an embedded CMYK profile** | PNG only supports RGB; CMYK data gets discarded, causing color shifts. | Convert to **RGB** before exporting PNGs. |
| **Using GIF for a full‑color photograph** | GIF’s 256‑color limit creates banding. | Choose **JPEG** for photographs; reserve GIF for simple graphics or animations. |
| **Forgetting to strip metadata** | Large file sizes due to EXIF data. | In **Save for Web**, set **Metadata** to **None**. |

---

## 8. Handy Shortcuts Recap  

| Action | Keyboard Shortcut (Windows) | Keyboard Shortcut (Mac) |
|--------|----------------------------|--------------------------|
| **Save As** | **Ctrl + Shift + S** | **Cmd + Shift + S** |
| **Export As** | **Alt + Shift + Ctrl + W** | **Option + Shift + Cmd + W** |
| **Save for Web** | **Alt + Shift + Ctrl + S** | **Option + Shift + Cmd + S** |
| **Duplicate Document** | **Ctrl + J** (while the document is active) | **Cmd + J** |

Memorizing these shortcuts will speed up the final stages of any project, allowing you to focus on creative tweaks rather than hunting through menus.

---

## Key Takeaways  

- **PSD** is your master file; always keep it untouched for future edits.  
- **JPEG**, **PNG**, and **GIF** each serve distinct web purposes—choose based on color depth, transparency, and animation needs.  
- **Resolution** matters: **72 dpi** for web (fast loading), **300 dpi** for print (sharp output).  
- **RGB** is for screens; **CMYK** is for printers. Convert color modes before the final export.  
- Use **Export As** for a quick, modern workflow; fall back to **Save for Web** when you need fine‑grained control over metadata and color profiles.  
- Optimize file size by resizing, selecting the proper format, adjusting quality/compression, and stripping unnecessary metadata.  
- Follow a consistent checklist: save PSD → duplicate → set correct mode/resolution → export with appropriate settings → organize files.  

By mastering these export and save techniques, you’ll deliver polished, appropriately sized images for any web or print project—ready for a client’s website or a professional press run. Happy exporting!

modules.title: 9. Mini Project: Create a Social Media Post
modules.content:
## From Blank Canvas to Instagram-Ready Post

Imagine this: it’s Tuesday evening, and your favorite café just dropped a new seasonal drink. You snap a photo with your phone, but the lighting is flat, the background is cluttered, and the text that should go on the image hasn’t even been created yet. In less than an hour, you could turn that raw photo into a polished social media post—ready to share with thousands of followers. With Photoshop, that transformation is not just possible; it’s repeatable, even for beginners.

This chapter isn’t about theory. You’ve already learned how to navigate the workspace, manage layers, adjust colors, and use masks and text. Now, you’ll apply those skills in one fluid workflow to create a single, shareable Instagram graphic. By the end, you’ll have a high-quality JPEG that looks intentional, not accidental—and you’ll understand how each step connects to what you’ve already practiced.

---

### ## Set the Stage: A 1080×1080 Canvas with Purpose

Instagram is a visual platform, and the square format (1:1) is still a classic choice, especially for brand posts or personal feeds emphasizing balance. A 1080×1080 pixel canvas is the standard for high-quality Instagram posts, ensuring your image looks sharp on both mobile and desktop screens.

**Why 1080×1080?**
- It’s Instagram’s default upload size for square posts.
- It avoids pixelation when viewed on high-resolution screens.
- It fits neatly into Instagram’s feed without awkward cropping.

**How to set it up:**
1. Open Photoshop.
2. Go to **File > New**.
3. In the dialog box:
   - Name your project: “AutumnLatte_Post”
   - Set **Width** to 1080 pixels and **Height** to 1080 pixels.
   - Set **Resolution** to 72 pixels per inch (ppi). While 300 ppi is ideal for print, 72 ppi is standard for web and social media.
   - Color Mode: **RGB Color** (for screen display).
   - Background Contents: **White** (a clean start).
4. Click **Create**.

You now have a blank 1080×1080 canvas. Notice the **Layers Panel** on the right—it’s empty, ready for your first layer.

---

### ## Bring in the Photo: Import, Crop, and Position

You’ve got your photo, but it might not be perfect. Maybe the subject is off-center, or the lighting is too dim. Let’s fix that.

**Step 1: Import the image**
Go to **File > Open**, select your photo, and click **Open**. The image opens in a new tab. To move it into your project, use the **Move Tool (V)** from the toolbar. Click and drag the image onto your 1080×1080 canvas.

**Step 2: Resize and reposition**
With the photo layer selected in the Layers Panel:
- Press **Ctrl+T** (Windows) or **Cmd+T** (Mac) to activate **Free Transform**.
- Hold **Shift** to maintain proportions while dragging a corner handle to resize.
- Drag inside the bounding box to reposition the image so the main subject sits comfortably within the frame.

**Tip:** Use the **Options Bar** at the top to set specific dimensions if you want precision.

**Step 3: Crop for composition**
If the photo still feels busy, use the **Crop Tool (C)** to trim excess space. Drag the corners to frame only what matters. Press **Enter** to confirm.

Now your photo sits on the canvas, but the background is still white. That’s fine—you’ll work with transparency and masks next.

---

### ## Refine with Masks: Isolate the Subject

The white background is too plain. You want the photo to blend naturally with any text or graphics you’ll add. Instead of erasing pixels, use a **mask** to hide parts of the image non-destructively.

**What is a mask?**
A mask acts like a stencil. Where the mask is black, the layer is hidden. Where it’s white, the layer is visible. You can paint with shades of gray for partial transparency.

**How to apply a mask:**
1. Select the photo layer in the Layers Panel.
2. Click the **Layer Mask** icon (rectangle with a circle) at the bottom of the Layers Panel.
3. A white mask thumbnail appears next to your photo.

Now, grab the **Brush Tool (B)**.
- Set **Brush Size** to 100 px and **Hardness** to 0% for soft edges.
- Set **Opacity** to 50% to make gradual changes.
- Choose black as your foreground color (press **D** to reset, then **X** to swap to black).

Paint over areas you want to hide—like the background or clutter. Use white (press **X**) to reveal parts that were accidentally hidden.

**Pro tip:** Zoom in (Ctrl/Cmd + +) to work on fine details like hair or edges.

---

### ## Set the Mood: Adjustment Layers for Color and Tone

Your photo might still lack pop. Adjustment layers let you tweak colors and contrast without harming the original image.

**Add a Vibrance adjustment:**
1. Click the **Adjustment Layer** icon (half-black, half-white circle) in the Layers Panel.
2. Choose **Vibrance**.
3. Increase **Vibrance** to +30 and **Saturation** to +15. This boosts muted colors without oversaturating skin tones.

**Add a Curves adjustment for contrast:**
1. Add another adjustment layer and choose **Curves**.
2. Click on the curve line to create a point. Drag it slightly upward in the middle to brighten midtones. Drag the ends downward slightly to deepen shadows.
3. Keep changes subtle—the goal is to enhance, not overpower.

**Tip:** Adjustment layers are non-destructive. Toggle their visibility (eye icon) to compare before and after.

---

### ## Add Your Message: Text That Pops

Text turns a photo into a post. But plain text on a photo can disappear. Use **layer styles** to make it stand out.

**Step 1: Add text**
Select the **Type Tool (T)**.
- Click on the canvas and type: “Sip the Season.”
- In the **Options Bar**, set the font to **Montserrat Bold** (or any bold sans-serif), size 60 pt, color #ffffff (white).
- Center-align the text using the alignment buttons in the Options Bar.

**Step 2: Style the text with layer effects**
Double-click the text layer in the Layers Panel to open **Layer Style**.
- Check **Drop Shadow**: set **Opacity** to 60%, **Distance** to 5 px, **Spread** to 0, **Size** to 10 px.
- Check **Stroke**: set **Size** to 2 px, **Position** to Outside, **Color** to black.
- Check **Gradient Overlay**: set **Style** to Linear, **Angle** to 90°, and choose a soft blue-to-white gradient.

These effects make the text readable against any background color.

**Step 3: Position the text**
Use the **Move Tool (V)** to place the text in a balanced spot—usually near the top or bottom third of the image.

---

### ## Add Flair: Vector Graphics and Icons

A single icon can speak louder than words. Use the **Shape Tools** to add a subtle graphic.

**Add a coffee cup icon:**
1. Select the **Custom Shape Tool (U)**.
2. In the Options Bar, click the shape thumbnail and choose a coffee cup icon (or any relevant symbol).
3. Click and drag to draw the shape on the canvas.
4. In the Layers Panel, rename the layer to “Coffee Icon.”

**Style the icon:**
Double-click the layer to open Layer Style.
- Add a **Color Overlay** of #d4a574 (a warm brown).
- Add a **Drop Shadow** with low opacity for depth.

Resize and position the icon near the text for visual balance.

---

### ## Polish and Preview

Before exporting, take a final look:
- Zoom out (Ctrl/Cmd -) to see the whole composition.
- Toggle layer visibility to check each element.
- Ensure text is readable at thumbnail size—squint if needed.

---

### ## Export as High-Quality JPEG

Instagram accepts JPEG files, but quality matters.

1. Go to **File > Export > Save for Web (Legacy)**.
2. In the dialog box:
   - Choose **JPEG** from the dropdown.
   - Set **Quality** to 100 (maximum).
   - Check **Embed Color Profile**: sRGB IEC61966-2.1 (standard for web).
   - Set **Progressive** to None.
3. Click **Save**.
4. Name the file: “AutumnLatte_Post.jpg” and choose a location.

Your file is now ready to upload to Instagram. The JPEG is high-quality, optimized for the web, and maintains the colors you set.

---

## Key Takeaways

- Use a **1080×1080 px canvas** with 72 ppi RGB color mode for Instagram square posts.
- Import and **resize** photos using **Free Transform (Ctrl/Cmd+T)** while holding **Shift** to maintain proportions.
- Apply **layer masks** to hide or reveal parts of an image non-destructively—paint with black to hide, white to reveal.
- Enhance photos with **adjustment layers** like Vibrance and Curves for subtle, effective color and contrast changes.
- Add and style **text** using the Type Tool and **layer styles** (Drop Shadow, Stroke, Gradient Overlay) for readability and visual appeal.
- Include **vector graphics** (shapes) to add icons or symbols—style them with layer effects for cohesion.
- Export as a **high-quality JPEG** via **Save for Web (Legacy)** at 100% quality with sRGB color profile for optimal Instagram uploads.

# Chapter 1: 1. Getting Started: Interface & Workspace

## A First‑Look at Photoshop

Imagine you’ve just taken a photo of a sunrise that you want to turn into a striking social‑media header. You launch Photoshop, stare at a sea of icons, and wonder where to begin. The truth is, before you start drawing or retouching, you need to understand the **workspace**—the digital desk where every tool lives. This chapter walks you through every pane and button you’ll meet the first time you open Photoshop, shows you how to arrange them for a workflow that feels natural, and teaches the essential navigation tricks that let you move around your image with confidence. By the end, you’ll be able to open a file, zoom in on a detail, pan across the canvas, and save your work as a Photoshop Document (**.psd**)—the foundation for everything that follows.

---

## The Menu Bar: Your Command Center

At the very top of the screen sits the **Menu Bar**. Think of it as the “File → Edit → Image” ladder you can climb to access every function Photoshop offers. Each menu groups related commands, and most actions you’ll perform later—such as creating a new document, adjusting image size, or applying a filter—are found here.

| Menu | Primary Purpose | Typical First‑Time Use |
|------|----------------|------------------------|
| **File** | Create, open, close, and save documents | *File → New* to start a blank canvas |
| **Edit** | Undo/redo, cut/copy/paste, transform selections | *Edit → Transform* to resize a layer |
| **Image** | Adjust overall image properties (size, rotation, mode) | *Image → Image Size* to change resolution |
| **Layer** | Manage layers, create masks, blending options | *Layer → New → Layer* to add a blank layer |
| **Select** | Make, modify, and save selections | *Select → All* to highlight the whole canvas |
| **Filter** | Apply creative or corrective effects | *Filter → Blur → Gaussian Blur* for softening |
| **View** | Control what you see (rulers, guides, zoom) | *View → Show → Grid* to display a grid overlay |
| **Window** | Show or hide panels (Tools, Layers, Color, etc.) | *Window → Layers* to bring the Layers panel back |
| **Help** | Access Photoshop help topics and tutorials | *Help → Photoshop Help* for on‑demand guidance |

> **Tip:** Hovering over any menu item highlights a short description at the bottom of the screen. Use this “status bar” as a quick reference while you explore.

---

## The Options Bar: Contextual Controls

Directly beneath the Menu Bar is the **Options Bar**. Unlike the static Menu Bar, the Options Bar changes its contents depending on the tool you have selected. It provides the most immediate controls for that tool, letting you fine‑tune settings without digging into dialogs.

### What You’ll See

- **Brush Size & Hardness** when the Brush tool is active.
- **Opacity & Flow** for any painting or erasing tool.
- **Blend Mode** dropdown for layers (e.g., *Multiply*, *Screen*).
- **Shape Options** (fill, stroke) when a shape tool is chosen.

### Why It Matters

Because the Options Bar reflects the **current context**, you can see at a glance what parameters are affecting your work. Adjusting the **Opacity** to 50 % makes a brush stroke semi‑transparent, which is essential for creating subtle shading or building up color gradually.

---

## The Tools Panel: The Toolbox

Located on the left side of the default workspace, the **Tools Panel** houses the icons you’ll click to select drawing, selection, and navigation tools. Each tool is represented by a small picture (an icon) and often has a keyboard shortcut for faster access.

| Tool | Icon Description | Shortcut | Typical Use |
|------|------------------|----------|-------------|
| **Move** | Four‑arrow cross | **V** | Reposition layers or selections |
| **Marquee** (Rectangular/Elliptical) | Dashed rectangle/ellipse | **M** | Select rectangular or oval areas |
| **Lasso** (Lasso, Polygonal, Magnetic) | Free‑hand line | **L** | Draw custom selections |
| **Crop** | Two intersecting right angles | **C** | Trim edges of an image |
| **Eyedropper** | Pipette tip | **I** | Sample a color from the canvas |
| **Brush** | Paintbrush tip | **B** | Paint or paint‑like effects |
| **Eraser** | Rectangular eraser | **E** | Remove paint or mask pixels |
| **Hand** | Open palm | **H** | Pan (move) the view when zoomed |
| **Zoom** | Magnifying glass | **Z** | Zoom in/out of the canvas |

> **Note:** The Tools Panel can be collapsed or expanded by clicking the double‑arrow at its top. If you ever lose it, press **Tab** to hide all panels, then **Shift + Tab** to bring them back.

### Customizing the Tools Panel

You can **reorder** tools by dragging their icons, and you can **hide** tools you never use. Right‑click the panel’s header and choose *Customize Toolbar* to add shortcuts or reset to the default layout.

---

## The Layers Panel: The Stack of Your Work

On the right side of the screen sits the **Layers Panel**. Photoshop works on the principle of **layers**, which are like transparent sheets stacked on top of each other. Each layer can hold its own image data, text, or adjustment, and you can edit a layer without affecting the others.

### Core Components

- **Layer Thumbnail** – a miniature preview of the layer’s content.
- **Eye Icon** – toggles visibility; click to hide/show a layer.
- **Lock Icon** – prevents accidental changes; useful for background layers.
- **Opacity Slider** – controls the transparency of the whole layer.
- **Blend Mode Dropdown** – determines how the layer mixes with layers beneath it (e.g., *Overlay* adds contrast).

### Basic Layer Operations

1. **Create a New Layer** – Click the **New Layer** button (paper‑plus icon) or press **Shift + Ctrl + N** (Windows) / **Shift + Cmd + N** (Mac).
2. **Rename a Layer** – Double‑click the layer’s name (e.g., “Layer 1”) and type a descriptive title.
3. **Reorder Layers** – Drag a layer up or down to change its stacking position.
4. **Group Layers** – Select multiple layers, then click the **Folder** icon to create a group, keeping related layers together.

Understanding layers early on will save you countless hours later, as most editing tasks rely on manipulating them rather than altering the original image.

---

## Customizing the Workspace

Photoshop ships with several preset workspaces—*Essentials*, *Photography*, *Graphic and Web*, etc.—but you can tailor the layout to match your personal workflow. A well‑organized workspace reduces mouse‑travel, keeps the tools you need in sight, and speeds up learning.

### Step‑by‑Step Customization

1. **Show/Hide Panels**  
   - Go to **Window** in the Menu Bar.  
   - Click any panel name (e.g., *Color*, *History*) to toggle its visibility.  
   - Panels you open will dock on the right side by default; you can drag them to the left or float them as separate windows.

2. **Arrange Panels**  
   - Drag a panel’s tab to a new location.  
   - Drop it when you see a blue highlight indicating where it will dock.  
   - Create tab groups by dropping one panel onto another’s tab.

3. **Resize Panels**  
   - Hover over a panel’s edge until the cursor changes to a double‑arrow.  
   - Click and drag to make the panel wider or taller.

4. **Save Your Layout**  
   - Once you’re happy with the arrangement, choose **Window → Workspace → New Workspace…**  
   - Give it a name (e.g., “My Beginner Setup”).  
   - Check the boxes for *Workspace*, *Keyboard Shortcuts*, and *Menu* if you also want to preserve any custom shortcuts.  
   - Click **Save**.  

   Later, you can switch back to this layout anytime via **Window → Workspace → My Beginner Setup**.

### Quick‑Access Tips

- **Resetting to Default** – If you ever get lost, choose **Window → Workspace → Essentials** and then click **Reset Essentials**.
- **Full‑Screen Mode** – Press **F** to toggle between normal, full‑screen with menu bar, and full‑screen without menu bar. This removes distractions while you focus on the canvas.

---

## Navigating the Canvas: Zoom, Pan, and Hand Tools

Even the simplest image can become a maze when you zoom in to edit fine details. Photoshop offers several navigation tools that let you move around without altering the image itself.

### Zoom Tool (**Z**)

- **Click** once to zoom **in** (default 200 %).  
- **Alt‑click** (Windows) / **Option‑click** (Mac) to zoom **out**.  
- **Click‑drag** to draw a rectangle around the area you want to fill the screen with.  

> **Pro tip:** Hold **Ctrl** (Windows) / **Cmd** (Mac) while scrolling the mouse wheel to zoom continuously.

### Hand Tool (**H**)

- Activate the Hand tool, then **click‑drag** anywhere on the canvas to pan (move) the view.  
- When you’re zoomed in, you’ll often switch rapidly between **Zoom** and **Hand**.  

> **Shortcut trick:** While the **Zoom** tool is active, press the **Spacebar** to temporarily switch to the Hand tool. Release the spacebar to return to Zoom.

### Pan Using Scrollbars

If you prefer not to use the Hand tool, you can also click the horizontal or vertical scrollbars at the bottom and right edges of the canvas. However, the Hand tool is usually faster for precise navigation.

### Fitting the Image to the Screen

- **Fit on Screen** – Press **Ctrl + 0** (Windows) / **Cmd + 0** (Mac).  
- **Actual Pixels** – Press **Ctrl + Alt + 0** (Windows) / **Cmd + Option + 0** (Mac) to view the image at 100 % size.

---

## Opening, Closing, and Saving PSD Files

A **PSD** (Photoshop Document) is Photoshop’s native file format. It preserves all layers, masks, adjustment layers, and vector information, allowing you to return to a project later and continue editing.

### Opening a File

1. Choose **File → Open…** or press **Ctrl + O** (Windows) / **Cmd + O** (Mac).  
2. In the dialog, navigate to the folder containing your image.  
3. Select a **.psd** file, or any other supported format (JPEG, PNG, TIFF).  
4. Click **Open**.  
   - If the file contains multiple layers, they appear in the Layers panel exactly as they were saved.  

### Closing a Document

- **File → Close** or press **Ctrl + W** (Windows) / **Cmd + W** (Mac).  
- If you have unsaved changes, Photoshop prompts you to **Save**, **Don’t Save**, or **Cancel**.  

### Saving Your Work

1. **Save** – Choose **File → Save** or press **Ctrl + S** (Windows) / **Cmd + S** (Mac). This overwrites the existing file.  
2. **Save As** – To create a new version or change the file type, select **File → Save As…**  
   - In the dialog, give the file a new name if desired.  
   - Choose **Photoshop (*.PSD; *.PDD)** from the format dropdown to retain layers.  
   - Click **Save**.  

   > **Important:** Saving as a JPEG or PNG flattens the image—layers are merged, and you lose the ability to edit them later. Always keep a master **.psd** version.

3. **Version Control** – For beginners, a simple habit helps: after each major edit, use **Save As** with an incremental suffix (e.g., *sunrise_v01.psd*, *sunrise_v02.psd*). This creates a safety net and lets you compare versions.

### Quick‑Save Shortcut

- Press **Ctrl + Shift + S** (Windows) / **Cmd + Shift + S** (Mac) to open the **Save As** dialog instantly.

---

## Putting It All Together: A Mini Workflow

1. **Launch Photoshop** – The default **Essentials** workspace appears.  
2. **Open your sunrise photo** – *File → Open* → select *sunrise.jpg*.  
3. **Zoom in** to the horizon line – press **Ctrl + +** (or use the Zoom tool).  
4. **Pan** to the left edge – hold **Spacebar** (temporary Hand tool) and drag.  
5. **Create a new layer** – **Shift + Ctrl + N**, name it *Adjustment*, and click **OK**.  
6. **Select the Brush tool** – press **B**, choose a soft brush from the Options Bar, set **Opacity** to 30 %.  
7. **Paint** a subtle orange highlight on the sun.  
8. **Save** – *File → Save As*, name it *sunrise_edit.psd*, keep the PSD format.  

You have now navigated the canvas, used a tool, worked with layers, and saved a fully editable Photoshop file. All of this was possible because you understood where each piece of the interface lives and how to customize it for your needs.

---

## Key Takeaways

- The **Menu Bar** houses all commands; the **Options Bar** shows tool‑specific settings; the **Tools Panel** provides quick access to drawing and selection tools; the **Layers Panel** manages the stack of editable elements.
- You can **customize** panel arrangement, hide or show panels, and **save** a personal workspace for future sessions.
- **Zoom**, **Hand**, and **Pan** tools let you navigate any canvas size; shortcuts like **Ctrl + 0** (fit) and **Spacebar** (temporary hand) speed up the process.
- Opening, closing, and **saving as PSD** preserves every layer and adjustment, ensuring you can return to a project without loss of editability.
- Practicing the workflow—open a file, zoom, pan, create a new layer, make a simple edit, and save—builds the muscle memory essential for every Photoshop project.

---

# Chapter 2: 2. Understanding Layers & Selections

### A Real‑World Problem: Fixing a Photo Without Damaging the Original  

You’ve just taken a portrait of a friend, but the background is distracting. You want to blur it while keeping the subject sharp, and you also need to brighten the eyes. The safest way to do this is to work on separate **layers** and use **selections** to isolate the parts you’re editing. By the end of this chapter you’ll know exactly how to set up those layers, name and organize them, and pick out the subject with the selection tools—all without ever altering the original image file.

---

## Why Layers Are the Backbone of Non‑Destructive Editing  

When you open a file in Photoshop you’re actually looking at a **canvas** that can hold many transparent sheets stacked on top of each other – those sheets are *layers*. Each layer can hold its own pixels, text, or adjustment, and you can change one layer without affecting the others. This is what makes Photoshop a **non‑destructive** editor: the original image stays intact, and you can always go back, tweak, or delete any change you’ve made.

* **Safety:** Mistakes are reversible.  
* **Flexibility:** Reorder layers to change the visual hierarchy.  
* **Control:** Apply blending modes, opacity, or filters to a single layer only.  

Think of layers like a stack of transparent acetate sheets in a studio. You can draw on the top sheet, erase it, or move it aside, and the drawing underneath never changes.

---

## The Layer Panel: Your Command Center  

If you followed the first chapter, you’ve already seen the **Layers Panel** on the right side of the workspace. It lists every layer in the current **.psd** file, showing a thumbnail, the layer name, and icons for visibility, lock status, and blending mode.

### Core Icons at a Glance  

| Icon | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| 👁️ | **Visibility** – click to hide/show the layer. |
| 🔒 | **Lock** – prevents accidental edits (can lock position, transparency, or all). |
| 🎚️ | **Opacity** – dim the layer’s overall strength (0 % – 100 %). |
| ⬜ | **Blend Mode** – determines how the layer mixes with those below (e.g., *Multiply*, *Screen*). |

Hovering over an icon shows a tooltip that tells you its function. You’ll use these icons constantly when you create, rename, reorder, hide, lock, and delete layers.

---

## Creating, Renaming, and Reordering Layers  

### 1. Adding a New Layer  

1. Click the **Create a new layer** icon (the sheet‑of‑paper button) at the bottom of the Layers Panel.  
2. A blank layer appears above the currently selected layer and is automatically named *Layer 1*.  

> **Tip:** If you want the new layer to inherit the blending mode or opacity of the layer beneath it, hold **Alt** (Windows) / **Option** (macOS) while clicking the icon.  

### 2. Renaming for Clarity  

1. Double‑click the layer’s name in the panel.  
2. Type a descriptive name (e.g., *Background Blur*, *Eyes Brightness*) and press **Enter**.  

> **Why rename?** Clear names let you locate a layer quickly, especially in projects with dozens of them.

### 3. Changing the Stack Order  

* **Drag‑and‑drop:** Click a layer and drag it up or down the list.  
* **Keyboard shortcuts:**  
  * **Ctrl + ]** (Windows) / **Cmd + ]** (macOS) → move the selected layer up one spot.  
  * **Ctrl + [** / **Cmd + [** → move it down.  

The order determines which layers cover others. The topmost layer is drawn last, so it appears in front.

---

## Hiding, Locking, and Deleting Layers  

### Visibility  

Click the eye icon to toggle a layer’s visibility. This is useful for checking how an edit looks without the layer’s influence.

### Locking  

Photoshop offers three lock options:  

| Lock Type | What It Does |
|-----------|--------------|
| **Transparency** | Prevents erasing or painting on transparent pixels. |
| **Image Pixels** | Stops any pixel changes (paint, erase, filters). |
| **Position** | Stops moving the layer with the Move tool. |
| **All** | Combines the three above. |

To lock, click the lock icon and choose the appropriate option from the dropdown.

### Deleting  

Select the layer and press **Delete** on the keyboard, or click the **Delete layer** trash‑can icon at the bottom of the panel. Photoshop will ask for confirmation if the layer contains content.

> **Caution:** Deleting a layer is permanent unless you undo (**Ctrl + Z** / **Cmd + Z**) immediately. For safety, consider hiding the layer first to see the effect before removing it.

---

## Non‑Destructive Editing with Adjustment Layers (A Quick Glimpse)  

While adjustment layers belong to a later chapter, it’s worth noting that they are themselves layers that apply color or tonal changes **without altering the pixels beneath**. Because they sit in the layer stack, you can enable/disable, reorder, or delete them at any time—another demonstration of Photoshop’s non‑destructive power.

---

## Selections: Isolating Parts of Your Image  

A **selection** is a temporary mask that tells Photoshop which pixels to affect. Anything outside the selection is ignored until you change or deselect it.

### Why Selections Matter  

* **Targeted edits:** Apply filters, adjustments, or paint only where you need them.  
* **Precision:** Combine simple shapes to outline complex objects.  
* **Efficiency:** Work faster by selecting once and applying multiple edits.

---

## The Three Core Selection Tools  

You already know the **Move**, **Marquee**, and **Lasso** tools from the first chapter. Here’s how they behave when you use them for selections.

### 1. Marquee Tools  

* **Rectangular Marquee** – creates a rectangular or square selection.  
* **Elliptical Marquee** – creates an oval or circular selection.  

**How to use:**  
1. Choose the tool from the Tools Panel.  
2. Click and drag on the canvas.  
3. Release the mouse to fix the selection.  

Hold **Shift** while dragging to constrain the shape (square or circle). Hold **Alt** (Windows) / **Option** (macOS) to draw from the centre outward.

### 2. Lasso Tools  

* **Lasso** – freehand drawing of any shape.  
* **Polygonal Lasso** – click to create straight‑line segments; double‑click to close.  
* **Magnetic Lasso** – snaps to edges with high contrast, great for objects with clear outlines.  

**How to use the Magnetic Lasso:**  
1. Click a point on the edge you want to trace.  
2. Move the cursor along the edge; Photoshop automatically adds points when the contrast changes.  
3. Click again to add a manual point if needed, or press **Enter** to close the selection.  

### 3. The Move Tool (When Paired with Selections)  

When a selection is active, the **Move tool** lets you reposition only the selected pixels. This is handy for aligning objects without affecting the rest of the image.

---

## Building a Selection Step by Step  

Let’s walk through selecting the subject’s face in a portrait.

1. **Start with the Elliptical Marquee**  
   * Choose the Elliptical Marquee tool.  
   * Hold **Shift** + **Alt** and drag from the center of the face outward to get a perfect circle that roughly covers the head.  

2. **Refine with the Lasso**  
   * Switch to the **Polygonal Lasso**.  
   * Click at the jawline, then at the chin, and finally back at the starting point to add the lower contour.  

3. **Add the Hair**  
   * Activate the **Magnetic Lasso**.  
   * Click just above the forehead and trace along the hairline. The tool will cling to the edge of the hair.  

4. **Combine the Shapes**  
   * As you add new paths, Photoshop automatically **adds to** the existing selection (the default mode).  

5. **Fine‑Tune**  
   * Press **Q** to enter **Quick Mask mode** (a red overlay appears).  
   * Use a soft brush to paint over areas you want to include (white) or exclude (black).  
   * Press **Q** again to exit; your refined selection is ready.  

> **Tip:** If you accidentally include too much, hold **Alt** (Windows) / **Option** (macOS) while using a selection tool to **subtract** from the current selection.

---

## Selection Modifiers: Adding, Subtracting, Intersecting  

Photoshop lets you change how a new selection interacts with the existing one. The **Options Bar** (just below the menu bar) contains three icons for this purpose:

| Icon | Action |
|------|--------|
| ![Add to selection icon] | **Add to** – new area is added to the current selection. |
| ![Subtract from selection icon] | **Subtract from** – new area is removed from the current selection. |
| ![Intersect with selection icon] | **Intersect with** – only the overlapping region remains selected. |

You can also use keyboard shortcuts:  

* **Shift** → *Add to*  
* **Alt** (Windows) / **Option** (macOS) → *Subtract from*  
* **Ctrl** (Windows) / **Cmd** (macOS) → *Intersect with*  

### Practical Example: Selecting a Person Wearing a Hat  

1. **Select the hat** with the Elliptical Marquee (Add to).  
2. **Switch to Subtract** and use the Polygonal Lasso to cut out the interior of the hat where the head shows.  
3. **Switch to Intersect** and draw a rough rectangle around the whole figure; only the overlapping area (the hat plus head) stays selected.  

Now you have a clean selection that isolates the entire subject.

---

## Managing Selections: Saving, Loading, and Deselecting  

### Saving a Selection  

1. With the selection active, go to **Select > Save Selection…**.  
2. In the dialog, give it a name (e.g., *SubjectMask*) and click **OK**.  
3. The selection is stored as an **alpha channel** in the Channels Panel, where you can reload it later via **Select > Load Selection…**.  

### Deselecting  

Press **Ctrl + D** (Windows) / **Cmd + D** (macOS) to remove the active selection.  

### Inverting a Selection  

If you need everything *except* the current area, choose **Select > Inverse** or press **Shift + Ctrl + I** / **Shift + Cmd + I**.

---

## Putting It All Together: A Mini Workflow  

Imagine you need to brighten the eyes and blur the background of a portrait.

1. **Create a new layer** above the background and name it *Background Blur*.  
2. **Select the background**:  
   * Use the Elliptical Marquee to roughly cover the whole image.  
   * Switch to Subtract and use the Lasso to carve out the subject’s head and shoulders.  
3. **Apply a blur**:  
   * With the background selected, go to **Filter > Blur > Gaussian Blur** and set a radius that looks natural.  
4. **Hide the selection** (Ctrl + D).  
5. **Create another new layer** named *Eyes Brightness*.  
6. **Select the eyes**:  
   * Zoom in, use the Polygonal Lasso to outline each eye, then hold **Shift** to add the second eye to the selection.  
7. **Adjust brightness**:  
   * Choose **Image > Adjustments > Brightness/Contrast** (or later, an adjustment layer) and increase the brightness slightly.  
8. **Toggle visibility** of each layer to compare the before/after effect.  

Because each edit lives on its own layer, you can now go back, change the blur amount, or delete the *Eyes Brightness* layer without touching the original photo.

---

## Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them  

| Issue | Why It Happens | Fix |
|-------|----------------|-----|
| **Accidentally painting on the wrong layer** | The wrong layer is selected or visible. | Always check the active layer highlighted in the Layers Panel before drawing or painting. |
| **Selection “jumps” when moving the mouse** | The selection mode (Add/Subtract/Intersect) is unintentionally changed. | Keep an eye on the **Options Bar** icons; press **Esc** to reset to *Add to* if unsure. |
| **Locked layers preventing edits** | The lock icon is engaged, often from a previous step. | Click the lock icon to unlock, or choose the specific lock type you need to disable. |
| **Too many layers cluttering the panel** | Every minor edit was made on a new layer without naming or grouping. | Rename layers descriptively, and later group related layers (right‑click → **Group from Layers**). |
| **Selections becoming “fuzzy” after scaling** | Scaling a layer after a selection can introduce anti‑aliasing artifacts. | Perform scaling before making the selection, or use **Smart Objects** (covered later). |

---

## Quick Reference Cheat Sheet  

- **Create layer:** `Shift + Ctrl + N` (Windows) / `Shift + Cmd + N` (macOS)  
- **Rename layer:** Double‑click name → type → `Enter`  
- **Hide/show layer:** Click eye icon or press `Alt + click` on eye to hide all others  
- **Lock layer:** Click lock icon → choose lock type  
- **Delete layer:** Select → `Delete` or click trash can  
- **Select all:** `Ctrl + A` / `Cmd + A`  
- **Deselect:** `Ctrl + D` / `Cmd + D`  
- **Add to selection:** Hold **Shift** while drawing  
- **Subtract from selection:** Hold **Alt** / **Option** while drawing  
- **Intersect selection:** Hold **Ctrl** / **Cmd** while drawing  
- **Quick Mask:** `Q` (enter/exit)  

---

## Practice Exercise  

1. Open a portrait of your choice.  
2. Create three layers named *Background Blur*, *Skin Smooth*, and *Eyes*.  
3. Use the selection tools and modifiers to isolate the background, the skin, and the eyes respectively.  
4. Apply a Gaussian blur to *Background Blur*, a **Surface Blur** (later chapter) to *Skin Smooth*, and increase the brightness of *Eyes*.  
5. Toggle each layer’s visibility to see the before/after effect.  

When you’re comfortable, experiment with renaming, reordering, and locking the layers to observe how the image changes.

## Frequently Asked Questions  

**Q: Can I select a layer directly without using a selection tool?**  
A: Yes. Click the layer’s thumbnail in the Layers Panel to make it active. If you need a pixel‑perfect selection of that layer’s opaque areas, hold **Ctrl** / **Cmd** and click the thumbnail; Photoshop will load a selection based on the layer’s transparency.

**Q: What’s the difference between a selection and a mask?**  
A: A selection is temporary and disappears when you deselect. A mask is a permanent (but editable) channel that lives with the layer. Masks will be covered in Chapter 5.

**Q: Why does the Lasso tool sometimes behave unpredictably?**  
A: The tool follows the cursor’s speed and pressure (if using a tablet). For smoother curves, try the **Pen tool** (covered later) or adjust the **tolerance** in the Options Bar for the Magnetic Lasso.

## Summary  

- Layers let you edit parts of an image independently, enabling non‑destructive workflows.  
- The Layers Panel is where you create, rename, reorder, hide, lock, and delete layers.  
- Selections define *where* edits happen; the Marquee, Lasso, and Move tools are your primary selection instruments.  
- Selection modifiers (add, subtract, intersect) let you combine simple shapes into complex selections.  
- Saving selections as channels preserves them for later use.  

By mastering layers and selections now, you’ll have a solid foundation for every Photoshop project that follows.

- **Create, rename, and reorder** layers to keep your workspace organized and intuitive.  
- **Hide or lock** layers to safeguard work and focus on specific elements.  
- **Marquee, Lasso, and Move** tools are the core instruments for making and adjusting selections.  
- Use **Shift, Alt/Option, and Ctrl/Cmd** to **add, subtract, or intersect** selections while drawing.  
- **Save selections** as alpha channels for reuse; **deselect** with **Ctrl + D / Cmd + D**.  
- Practicing a simple workflow—isolating background, skin, and eyes—will cement these concepts and prepare you for more advanced techniques later.

# Chapter 3: 3. Working with Colors & Brushes

## A Splash of Color: Why Choosing the Right Hue Matters  

Imagine you’ve just taken a photo of a sunrise and want to add a hand‑drawn “sun” that matches the warm tones of the sky. The difference between a flat orange circle and a vibrant, gradient‑rich sun is often just the way you pick and apply colors. In Photoshop, mastering **foreground** and **background** colors is the first step toward any creative brush work—whether you’re sketching, retouching, or adding simple accents.

---

## Selecting Colors  

Photoshop gives you three fast ways to tell the program which color you want to paint with. All three live in the **Tools Panel** and are reflected in the **Options Bar** at the top of the screen.

### 1. The Color Picker (Foreground/Background Swatches)  

1. **Locate the swatches** – In the lower part of the Tools Panel you’ll see two overlapping squares. The top (solid) square is the **foreground color** (the color you’ll paint with). The bottom (hollow) square is the **background color** (used by tools such as the Paint Bucket).  
2. **Open the Color Picker** – Click either swatch. A dialog called the **Color Picker** appears.  
3. **Choose a hue** –  
   * **Hue bar** (vertical on the right) selects the color family.  
   * **Saturation/value square** (large area) refines the exact shade.  
   * **Hexadecimal field** (bottom) lets you type a web color code (e.g., `#FF5733`).  
4. **Confirm** – Click **OK**. The swatch updates to show your new color.  

> **Tip:** Double‑click a swatch to open the Color Picker instantly, even if the tool you’re using isn’t a brush (e.g., the Eraser).

### 2. Swatches Panel – Quick Access to Favorites  

If you often reuse the same colors, the **Swatches** panel (Window → Swatches) is a visual palette of saved colors.

* **Add a swatch** – After picking a color with the Color Picker, click the **New Swatch** button at the bottom of the panel.  
* **Apply a swatch** – Simply click a swatch; the foreground color updates automatically.  
* **Organize** – Drag swatches to reorder them, or create groups for project‑specific palettes.  

> **Tip:** Photoshop ships with a set of “Web Safe” swatches. For print‑oriented work, you may want to create a custom set that matches your brand colors.

### 3. Eyedropper Tool – Grab Color Directly from the Image  

The **Eyedropper** (shortcut **I**) lets you sample any pixel on the canvas.

1. **Select the Eyedropper** from the Tools Panel.  
2. **Click** on the area whose color you want to capture. The foreground swatch instantly changes to that exact hue.  
3. **Sample multiple points** – Hold **Shift** and click additional spots; Photoshop will average the colors.  

> **Tip:** If you need a soft, blended sample (e.g., for a gradient sky), set the **Sample Size** in the Options Bar to **3 × 3** or **5 × 5** pixels.

---

## Getting Comfortable with the Brush Tool  

Now that you have a color, it’s time to bring it to life. The **Brush Tool** (shortcut **B**) is the workhorse for painting, retouching, and even creating masks.

### Accessing the Brush Settings Panel  

* **Open the panel** – Choose **Window → Brush Settings**.  
* **Why a separate panel?** – While the **Options Bar** lets you adjust size and hardness on the fly, the Brush Settings panel gives deeper control over shape, dynamics, texture, and more.

### Core Brush Controls  

| Setting | What It Does | Typical Use |
|---------|--------------|-------------|
| **Size** | Diameter of the brush tip (in pixels). | Large strokes for backgrounds, small for details. |
| **Hardness** | Edge sharpness (0 % = soft feathered edge, 100 % = crisp edge). | Soft edges for natural media effects; hard edges for graphic lines. |
| **Spacing** | Distance between consecutive brush marks when you drag. | Low spacing (1–5 %) for smooth lines; high spacing (10 %+) for dotted or stippled effects. |
| **Shape Dynamics** | Varies size, angle, or roundness based on pen pressure or direction. | Useful with graphics tablets for pressure‑sensitive brushwork. |
| **Texture** | Applies an image‑based texture to the brush tip. | Simulates charcoal, fabric, or custom patterns. |

> **Note:** Opacity and Flow are still controlled from the Options Bar. Opacity limits the overall transparency of each stroke, while Flow determines how quickly the paint builds up as you drag.

### Painting Simple Strokes – A Step‑by‑Step Walkthrough  

1. **Set your foreground color** – Use any of the three methods described earlier.  
2. **Select the Brush Tool** – Press **B** or click the brush icon.  
3. **Adjust size & hardness** –  
   * Quick change: Use the **[ ] brackets** on the keyboard (`[` reduces size, `]` increases).  
   * For finer control, click the **Size** or **Hardness** icons in the Options Bar and drag the sliders.  
4. **Create a stroke** – Click once to place a dot, or click‑drag to draw a line. Release the mouse button to finish.  
5. **Undo mistakes** – Press **Ctrl+Z** (Windows) or **Cmd+Z** (macOS) to step back.  

**Practice Exercise:**  
Create a small canvas (400 × 400 px). Paint a simple sun using a round brush (size ≈ 80 px, hardness ≈ 70 %). Then, switch to a soft brush (size ≈ 150 px, hardness ≈ 0 %) and add a subtle glow around the sun. This exercise demonstrates how size and hardness affect the feel of a stroke.

### Using the Eraser Tool  

The **Eraser** (shortcut **E**) works like a brush that paints with the **background color**—or, when you enable **“Use Brush”** mode, it behaves exactly like the Brush Tool but removes pixels instead of adding them.

1. **Select the Eraser** from the Tools Panel.  
2. **Choose a size & hardness** – The same shortcuts (`[` `]`) and Options Bar controls apply.  
3. **Erase** – Click‑drag over the area you want to clear. If you’re working on a **transparent layer**, the erased area becomes transparent (you’ll see the gray‑white checkerboard).  

> **Tip:** For precise erasing, switch the **Mode** in the Options Bar to **“Brush”** and turn on **“All Layers”** if you need to erase across multiple layers simultaneously.

---

## Crafting Your Own Brush Preset  

Photoshop ships with dozens of default brushes, but creating a custom brush lets you infuse your personal style into every project.

### Step‑by‑Step: Save a Custom Brush  

1. **Create the brush shape** –  
   * **Method A:** Use the **Brush Tool** with a unique size, hardness, and spacing.  
   * **Method B:** Convert any selection or shape into a brush. Draw a vector shape (e.g., a star) on a new layer, then go to **Edit → Define Brush**.  
2. **Open the Brush Settings panel** – Window → Brush Settings.  
3. **Fine‑tune** – Adjust **Shape Dynamics**, **Texture**, **Dual Brush**, or **Color Dynamics** to get the exact look you want.  
4. **Save the preset** – In the Brush Settings panel, click the **Create New Brush** icon (looks like a folded page) at the top right. A dialog appears:  
   * **Name** – Give it a descriptive name (e.g., “Soft Sunburst”).  
   * **Preset Manager** – Click **OK**. The new brush appears in the **Brush Preset Picker** (the dropdown next to the Brush Tool icon).  
5. **Organize** – Open **Window → Brush Presets**. You can drag your new brush into a custom group for easy access later.  

> **Tip:** If you plan to share the brush with others, select the brush in the preset picker, then click the **Export Selected Brushes** button (the little folder icon) to save a **.abr** file.

### Quick Checklist for a Good Custom Brush  

- **Consistent size** – Ensure the brush tip size aligns with the intended use (e.g., fine detail vs. broad background).  
- **Balanced hardness** – Soft edges for natural media, hard edges for graphic work.  
- **Appropriate spacing** – Set to 1 % for smooth strokes; increase for stipple or scatter effects.  
- **Naming convention** – Include the intended use (e.g., “Watercolor‑Wash‑Large”) to locate it quickly later.

---

## Putting It All Together: Mini Project  

**Goal:** Add a hand‑drawn highlight to a portrait photo.  

1. **Open a portrait** (`File → Open`).  
2. **Create a new layer** (`Layer → New → Layer…`) so your brush work stays non‑destructive.  
3. **Pick a highlight color** – Use the **Eyedropper** to sample a bright spot on the subject’s cheek, then shift the hue slightly toward a warmer tone using the Color Picker.  
4. **Select a soft round brush** – Size ≈ 30 px, hardness ≈ 0 %, low spacing.  
5. **Paint the highlight** – Click‑drag over the cheek, building up the color gradually. Adjust **Opacity** in the Options Bar to keep the effect subtle.  
6. **Refine** – Switch to a smaller, harder brush (size ≈ 10 px, hardness ≈ 80 %) to add a crisp edge where the light catches.  
7. **Erase excess** – Use the Eraser with a soft edge (size ≈ 50 px, hardness ≈ 0 %) to blend the painted area into the skin.  
8. **Save a custom brush** – If you liked the shape of the highlight stroke, define it as a brush for future portraits.  

This workflow demonstrates how color selection, brush adjustments, and erasing combine to produce a polished, realistic effect—all while keeping the original photo untouched on its own layer.

---

## Frequently Asked Beginner Questions  

| Question | Answer |
|----------|--------|
| **Can I change the background color while using the Brush Tool?** | Yes. Click the background swatch (the hollow square) to open the Color Picker, then paint with tools that reference the background (e.g., Paint Bucket). |
| **Why does my brush sometimes look “jagged” even at a high size?** | Check the **Spacing** setting. A high spacing value creates visible gaps. Reduce it to ≤ 5 % for a smooth line. |
| **Do I need a graphics tablet to use Shape Dynamics?** | Not strictly. Without a tablet, you can still vary size or angle by using the **Pen Pressure** option set to **“Off”** and manually adjusting the **Size Jitter** slider. |
| **What’s the difference between Opacity and Flow?** | Opacity limits the maximum transparency of each brush mark. Flow controls how quickly that opacity builds up as you drag. Think of Flow as “paint application speed.” |
| **Can I delete a custom brush I no longer need?** | Open the **Brush Presets** panel, right‑click the brush, and choose **Delete Brush**. Confirm the deletion. |

---

## Tips for Building Good Brush Habits  

- **Use keyboard shortcuts** (`[` `]` for size, **Shift+[`]** for hardness) to keep your flow uninterrupted.  
- **Preview brush changes** – In the Brush Settings panel, the preview window shows a live representation of your adjustments.  
- **Keep a “Color Reference” layer** – Duplicate a small portion of your image, lock the layer, and use it as a visual guide for consistent hue selection.  
- **Name layers descriptively** – When you start painting on a new layer, rename it (e.g., “Sun Highlights”) to stay organized, especially as you add multiple brush elements later.

## ## Key Takeaways  

- **Foreground vs. background colors** are set via the swatches; the foreground is what the Brush and Eraser tools paint with.  
- **Three primary color selection methods**: Color Picker (precise hue), Swatches panel (quick access to saved colors), and Eyedropper tool (sample directly from the canvas).
